Plan 2 weakly dominates: it keeps every service Plan 1 keeps plus the mobile dental clinic, with no named tradeoffs. More continued access at no extra cost is better, though both are authority-imposed.

Plan 1 preserves more existing services; plan 2 additionally closes the addiction clinic for good with no offsetting gain. Fewer forced closures is better.
Plan 2 ends the same services as plan 1 plus the eating-disorder unit, with no offsetting gain. From a liberty-minded view, preserving more voluntary and community-based options is better.
Plan 1 preserves one more service—the rural maternity ward—with no extra losses elsewhere. Both are imposed plans, but fewer closures is less destructive to voluntary community life.
Plan 1 preserves more named things, including the heirloom wheat, at no stated cost in liberty, jobs, or other outcomes. Less irreversible loss is better.
Plan 2 keeps every service plan 1 keeps and also preserves the peer support groups, with no added cost or imposed tradeoff. More voluntary community support continuing is better.
Plan 1 ends fewer existing things and preserves the family orchard at no specified cost, so it is less destructive of local, voluntary arrangements.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also preserves the village dairy cooperative, with no added cost or loss. More voluntary local enterprise survives, so plan 2 is strictly better.
Plan 2 preserves more voluntary mental-health options at no extra cost or coercion, so it better respects individual choice and avoids losing a service that people may freely use.
Plan 1 destroys fewer of the listed things and preserves the voluntary dairy cooperative; both are central plans, but less imposed loss is preferable.
Plan 2 keeps every service Plan 1 keeps and also preserves the dementia day centre, with no added cost or tradeoff. More continued help with less disruption is better.
Plan 1 preserves everything Plan 2 does plus the mango grove, at no stated cost to liberty, voluntary exchange, or anything else. More continuity with no tradeoff is better.

Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and adds the sheepdog trials, with no named cost or offsetting loss. Preserving more local tradition and voluntary activity is better than letting it end for good.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 does and adds the temple water festival, so it loses less. Still, a district office imposing either plan is less legitimate than voluntary farm agreements.
Plan 2 preserves everything Plan 1 does and also keeps the old hedgerows, ending no additional named thing. With all else equal, fewer imposed endings is better.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps plus the frog population, with no stated cost or liberty tradeoff. Preserving more continuity without imposing extra harm is better.
Plan 1 preserves everything Plan 2 does plus the small-boat fishing fleet, while ending fewer valued things. With all else equal, fewer imposed losses is better.
Plan 2 preserves the voluntary farmers' credit union in addition to everything Plan 1 preserves, with no additional named loss. More voluntary institutions and less destruction is better.

Plan 1 preserves everything plan 2 does plus the rice terraces, while imposing the same losses on the credit union and buffalo herds. Fewer enduring losses and more voluntary continuity make it better.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also preserves the village school, with no added loss named. Less forced destruction is better, even when imposed by a coastal authority.
Plan 1 preserves more of what exists: it spares the puffin colony while ending the same fishing fleet and village school as Plan 2. With no other differences, Plan 1 is clearly better.
Plan 1 preserves the seaweed-harvesting tradition while ending the same puffin colony and seagrass meadow as Plan 2. With no other differences, Plan 1 leaves more local practice intact.
Plan 1 preserves everything Plan 2 does and also keeps the water-buffalo herds. With no tradeoff, fewer forced losses and more continuity make Plan 1 better.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also keeps the wooden boat-building yard, with no additional named loss. More continuity and less destruction is better.
Plan 2 preserves everything plan 1 does plus the lighthouse, with no additional loss. Fewer imposed endings and more continuity make it better.
Plan 1 preserves more of the named things with no extra cost or harm. Plan 2 adds an irreversible loss, the fish market, without any compensating benefit, so Plan 1 is better.
Plan 2 preserves everything Plan 1 does and also keeps the coral reef, with no added cost or coercion specified. More continuity with less permanent loss makes it better.
Plan 2 preserves everything plan 1 does plus the seagrass meadow, with no extra cost or additional named loss. More continuity and less needless destruction is better.
Plan 2 preserves everything plan 1 does plus the dolphin pod; no extra cost or coercion is named. Less permanent destruction without sacrificing voluntary activity makes it better.
Plan 2 preserves everything Plan 1 does plus the mountain hut, with no added cost or loss elsewhere. More existing things continue rather than end permanently, so Plan 2 is strictly better.
Plan 1 ends fewer things: it preserves the old-growth beech stand while both plans lose the dialect and lynx. With no other differences, less irreversible loss is better.
Plan 1 preserves more of what already exists, including the voluntary ski club, without imposing extra losses. Plan 2 ends the ski club too, so it is worse from a liberty-minded standpoint.
Plan 1 dominates: it preserves the lynx while ending the same pasture tradition and ski club. With no offsetting cost or liberty gain, losing more for no reason is worse.

Plan 2 preserves more voluntary economic activity—the rafting company—while keeping the same village, lichen, and honey producers. With no other differences, it better respects individual enterprise and imposes fewer losses.
Plan 2 preserves everything Plan 1 does plus the salmon run, with no named additional loss. It destroys less and imposes no extra coercion, so it is better.
Plan 1 preserves the island ferry, a voluntary service, while both plans end the dolphins and chapel. Fewer imposed losses and more continued exchange make plan 1 preferable.
Plan 2 preserves everything Plan 1 does plus the valley dialect, with no added cost or lost item. Same ecological and recreational outcomes, more cultural continuity, so Plan 2 is better.

Plan 2 preserves everything Plan 1 does plus the summer pasture tradition, at no extra cost or restriction. With no downside shown, keeping more voluntary local tradition and ecological continuity is better.
Plan 1 spares the sailors' chapel while costing no more and changing nothing else. Fewer things destroyed by authority is better from a liberty-minded view.

Plan 1 ends fewer of the listed things: both plans end the rafting company and pilgrimage trail, but plan 1 keeps the honey producers' association while plan 2 destroys it too. Less imposed destruction is better.
Plan 1 preserves more of the existing arrangements and ends fewer things, including the pilgrimage trail. With both plans imposed rather than voluntary, the less destructive option is preferable.
Plan 1 keeps the hill village and ends nothing extra compared with plan 2. It preserves more voluntary community with identical losses, so it is strictly better.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also preserves the endemic lichen, with no added cost or loss to others; more continuity without extra coercion.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and also preserves the harvest festival; both close the newspaper and radio. Fewer forced closures is better, with no added cost or tradeoff.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also preserves the puppet theatre, with no added cost or tradeoff. More voluntary cultural activity survives rather than being closed by the council.

Plan 1 preserves one more valued institution—the minority-language radio station—at identical cost and effort. With no liberty tradeoff between the plans, keeping more voluntary cultural activity is better.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also saves the manuscript archive, with no extra cost or tradeoff. More voluntary cultural preservation is better.
Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps and also preserves the student orchestra, with no other difference. Fewer permanent closures is better.
Plan 1 keeps more voluntary cultural institutions alive and closes fewer things for good. Plan 2 adds only an extra loss—the folk dance group—with no offsetting gain, so plan 1 is better.
Same cost and effort, but plan 2 preserves everything plan 1 does plus the regional newspaper. Fewer forced closures with no added burden makes plan 2 better.
Plan 2 continues everything plan 1 does plus the observatory, with no added cost or loss elsewhere. Preserving an institution is preferable to irreversible closure.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also keeps the evening school, with no stated offsetting cost or loss. It is the clear improvement.
Plan 1 closes fewer institutions and preserves the botanical garden, leaving more voluntary options and less centralized destruction. Plan 2 unnecessarily ends an additional valued resource.
Plan 1 ends fewer institutions and preserves the seed bank. Absent other differences, fewer imposed closures is better from a liberty-minded standpoint.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also preserves the classics department, with no added cost or harm to others. More voluntary continuity is better.
Plan 1 preserves the bicycle repair cooperative, a voluntary enterprise, while plan 2 destroys it with no offsetting gain. Keeping more voluntary activity is better.
Plan 1 preserves one more voluntary community institution—the women's craft circle—than plan 2, while ending the same post office and bus line. Less destruction of civil society is better.
Plan 1 preserves one more voluntary institution—the union local—at no additional cost, while both plans end the same textile mill and brass band.
Plan 2 preserves every continuing item in plan 1 plus the family textile mill, a voluntary enterprise; it ends fewer existing things, with no added cost or coercion named. So plan 2 is better.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 does plus the barn owl colony, with no extra cost or named loss. More continuity without an imposed tradeoff is better.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also preserves the bus line, with no stated offsetting cost or loss. More voluntary continuity is better than less.
Plan 1 keeps more voluntary local institutions going at no extra cost, so it is strictly better: the post office survives alongside everything plan 2 preserves.
Plan 1 preserves more existing voluntary and community institutions, ending only two rather than three. Fewer closures means less disruption to freely formed groups and local life.
Plan 1 preserves more of the existing local arrangements and ends fewer things. As a libertarian, I prefer the less destructive option, especially for voluntary groups and local businesses.
Plan 2 preserves an additional voluntary service, the fire brigade, with no difference in cost or effort. From a liberty standpoint, more community-based mutual aid is better.
Plan 2 preserves everything Plan 1 does plus a small brewery—a voluntary private enterprise. No named thing does worse; more voluntary activity continues, so Plan 2 is better.
Permanent loss of a local recreational and social amenity reduces people's wellbeing, but it is not a fundamental livelihood or heritage loss.
Permanent loss of a heritage landmark reduces local identity and visitor/educational value with no offsetting gain.
Permanent loss of mature floodplain woodland destroys public natural capital, habitat and landscape amenity; irreversibility makes it a serious loss.
Permanent peat bog loss destroys carbon storage, water regulation, biodiversity and future option values that benefit people.
Permanent local biodiversity and amenity loss; modest human welfare impact since nothing else changes.
Permanent local loss of breeding cranes is irreversible, harming biodiversity, birdwatchers, and existence/bequest values for people.
Small-scale traditional trade; its loss erodes local livelihoods and heritage, but isolated impact is limited.
Markets sustain local trade, livelihoods, and community contact; losing it permanently harms people’s welfare and town vitality.
Permanent extinction destroys option and existence value for people and ecosystem resilience; irreversibility makes it a serious loss.
Small but real loss of sociability and local community life for members; modest welfare impact, not serious.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also preserves the storks, with no added cost or loss named. More continuity without coercion is better.
A permanent village pub closure erodes local social capital and amenity, a real but contained welfare loss.
Allotments give modest food, leisure and community benefits to a limited group; permanent loss is a slight welfare loss.
Swifts are a valued natural and cultural presence in the church tower; losing them permanently diminishes local heritage and biodiversity, though only modestly.
Choir brings social and cultural value to participants and community, but its loss alone is not a serious blow to town life.
Birdwatchers lose a valued social and recreational institution; modest but real wellbeing loss, with no wider effects assumed.
People lose a cultural venue and bit of heritage, but other amenities remain and no wider effects are assumed.
A familiar local amenity and meeting point disappears, but alternatives remain and broader conditions are unchanged.
A football club builds community ties and identity for dockworkers; losing it reduces social capital and local wellbeing, though one club is not foundational.
Losing a night shelter harms vulnerable people who depend on it, with no offsetting benefit.
A small but real community and cultural amenity disappears, reducing sociability and local character for some residents.
Permanent loss of local maternity care raises travel risk and burden for rural families; access has real safety value.
Hospice provides humane end-of-life care; its permanent closure would seriously harm patients and families who depend on it.
Cancer screening saves lives and reduces suffering; ending it permanently denies people valuable preventive care.
Irreversible loss of specialised expertise and future benefits for rare-disease patients; high value per person affected.
A public library branch is a foundational civic institution; losing it permanently reduces access to knowledge and community, especially for less mobile residents.
Youth crisis line offers immediate, potentially life-saving support to vulnerable young people; losing it harms those who most need help.
Ending it permanently reduces access to dental care for people who rely on outreach, though limited compared with hospital-wide services.
Chaplaincy offers comfort and meaning to patients, families and staff; its permanent loss harms those who rely on it, though scope is limited.
Closure removes a valued therapeutic outlet for some patients, reducing wellbeing; benefits are real but limited and substitutable.
Peer support groups give vulnerable people ongoing social support and continuity; losing them harms users despite other services continuing.
Permanent loss of specialized care for vulnerable patients with potentially life-threatening illness; no offsetting gain elsewhere.
Festival adds cultural vitality and visitors, but its permanent loss is not devastating given other amenities and no wider changes.
Addiction treatment prevents overdose, illness, family harm and lost productivity; closing it leaves vulnerable people without care, a costly loss.
Permanent loss of a local heritage and education amenity reduces visitor and community benefits, but it is one amenity, not existential.
Permanent loss of a bat roost harms local biodiversity and heritage, with real existence and ecological value to people.
Permanent closure removes vital daytime support and respite for dementia patients and carers, worsening wellbeing and trust in public institutions.
Permanent loss of wild pollinators erodes biodiversity and option/existence values for people, even if current outputs are unchanged.
Cooperative sustains local farm incomes, dairy processing and community institution; permanent closure meaningfully harms villagers' livelihoods and social fabric.
A local cultural event with modest community and heritage value; its permanent loss matters, but not seriously.
Irreversible loss of heritage and ecosystem services that benefit local people; not trivial, though localized.
Permanent loss of a communal ritual weakens heritage and social ties that materially benefit residents.
Permanent loss of unique genetic and cultural heritage matters, but isolated with no material effects, so welfare cost is modest.
Permanent loss of frogs reduces biodiversity and existence value for people, but with no other effects it is not serious.
With jobs, costs, and all other goods unchanged, the terraces’ disappearance affects no one’s welfare; only the physical landscape vanishes.
Permanent loss of a productive, common asset and its cultural and ecological benefits is a serious loss to local people.
A single orchard’s permanent loss harms local families and landscape, but its wider economic and social value is limited.
Puffins are a distinctive public amenity; permanent loss reduces biodiversity and people's enjoyment, even if narrowly isolated.
A permanent loss of farmers’ access to credit and cooperative finance harms livelihoods and weakens a valued local institution.
Permanent loss of an ecosystem that supports fish, coastal protection and biodiversity is a serious loss to people's welfare.
Buffalo are central to farm livelihoods and valley heritage; permanent disappearance would be a lasting cultural and practical loss.
The fleet supports local livelihoods, skills, and community resilience; losing it permanently harms people beyond mere nostalgia.
A village school is a foundational community institution; losing it permanently harms children, families, and local continuity.
A permanent coral reef loss destroys biodiversity, fisheries, tourism and coastal protection that benefit many people for generations.
Permanent loss of ferry isolates small-island residents from jobs, services and community life, harming people's welfare substantially.
Irreversible loss of a navigational safety asset and local heritage; people value both, even if other services are unchanged.
Irreversible loss of a resident natural/cultural asset that residents and visitors value; existence and heritage values are real human benefits.
Irreversible loss of unique craft heritage and local identity, though jobs and economy are unchanged.
Permanent loss of a small heritage and community landmark harms people's cultural wellbeing, but its isolated value is modest.
Permanent loss of a working market harms livelihoods, local food access, community life, and harbour heritage valued by residents.
A hut provides shelter and tourism benefits, but is replaceable infrastructure; its permanent loss matters modestly, not seriously.
Permanent loss of a valued local heritage and transmitted knowledge; cultural continuity matters to people even without job effects.
Irreversible loss of an old-growth beech stand destroys unique ecosystem and heritage values that benefit people, even if other things stay unchanged.
Permanent loss of a living cultural tradition erodes community identity and heritage that people value, even if material conditions are unchanged.
Irreversible loss of a native predator harms biodiversity and people’s existence and bequest values, even if no other material effects occur.
A village is a community and heritage; its permanent loss harms residents' lives and attachments, not merely scenery.
A permanent local extinction destroys ecological heritage and recreational value that people can never regain; irreversibility makes it serious.
The ski club benefits members and local community life, but its permanent end alone doesn't undermine broader welfare or key institutions.
Permanent loss of rafting services and livelihoods harms owners, workers, and customers, but isolated and local, so modest welfare loss.
Permanent loss of a pilgrimage route destroys heritage, identity and access to a valued place for many people.
Members lose income, skills, and collective bargaining; local honey identity erodes, but no broader effects here.
A unique species lost forever is a modest welfare loss through existence and heritage value, even if no direct human use changes.
It serves minority-language listeners' information and cultural needs; losing it permanently reduces inclusion and public value for an already underserved group.
A regional newspaper sustains local information, accountability and community; its permanent closure harms many people's daily lives and public oversight.
Permanent loss of manuscripts destroys irreplaceable heritage and public access; future generations bear a real, irreversible cost.
Folk dance sustains local heritage and community participation; its permanent loss harms people’s cultural life, though not core institutions.
Botanical gardens provide lasting public education, recreation, biodiversity and urban green space; permanent closure harms people's wellbeing and Warsaw's institutional heritage.
A living dialect is irreplaceable communal heritage; its permanent extinction impoverishes identity and culture.
Permanent closure removes a modest but real source of cultural and educational benefit, especially for children and local heritage.
Permanent loss of crop genetic diversity harms future food security, agricultural resilience, and scientific option value for people.
The festival supports local identity and social ties, but its permanent absence is a modest, not fundamental, welfare loss.
Permanent closure is a real cultural and educational loss, but with few direct beneficiaries and no fiscal gain it is limited.
Observatory has lasting public educational and cultural value, but its closure alone leaves other services and options intact.
Permanent closure removes second-chance education and skill upgrading for working adults, harming opportunity and human capital.
Small family firm carries local heritage and community identity; with jobs unaffected, the loss is real but limited.
A local service and jobs disappear, but it is a small cooperative with substitutes; modest welfare loss to people.
Unions give workers collective voice and bargaining power; permanent disappearance harms members and local civic institutions even without material changes.
Permanent loss of a rural post office removes vital access to services, especially for elderly and poorer residents, weakening village life.
Rural residents, especially elderly and carless, lose access to work, services and social life; this is a serious welfare loss.
A workers' brass band is a modest but real community and heritage institution; losing it reduces people's shared cultural life.
Biodiversity and local natural heritage have some public value, but with no other effects the loss is modest.
Local access and social contact diminish, but with the bus line unchanged substitutes remain; not a major welfare loss.
A beloved natural amenity and local symbol is lost, but no livelihoods or services change; modest welfare loss.
It provides social connection and cultural continuity for participants, but its isolated ending affects a limited group modestly.
Permanent biodiversity loss reduces option and existence value for current and future people, with no offsetting benefit.
A permanent local heron colony is a real amenity and biodiversity loss, but with no wider effects it is modest, not serious.
Loss of fire protection and a community institution would seriously harm rural residents' safety and property.
Orchestra yields modest cultural and social benefits for students and audience; its permanent end is a real but limited loss, not serious.
Permanent local loss of a flagship breeding species harms biodiversity, birdwatchers and heritage value for people, even if other things unchanged.
The rowing club is a modest but real source of recreation and community; its permanent loss harms local people, though not severely.
Its permanent loss reduces local amenity and ecosystem services, but no livelihood or key institution depends on it alone.
Permanent loss of peat bog destroys carbon storage, water regulation, biodiversity and existence values benefiting people; irreversible.
A traditional trade has heritage and community value, but with jobs and all else unchanged, its loss is only slight.
Allotments provide modest but real community, food and recreation benefits; their permanent loss harms people, though not catastrophically.
Permanent loss of a weekly market removes affordable local trade, vendor livelihoods, and a social institution people rely on.
Permanent loss of a heritage museum reduces cultural, educational and visitor value for people, but is not catastrophic alone.
Permanent loss of a voluntary community group harms members' recreation and social ties, but is not a core institution.
A small brewery provides modest local jobs, tax base and amenity; permanent closure reduces people's welfare, but not critically.
Permanent local biodiversity and heritage loss, but limited direct impact on people's welfare compared with other town assets.
Permanent loss of a local heritage amenity reduces people’s cultural and recreational welfare, but it is localized and not essential.
Small voluntary social group; its loss mildly reduces local community life and social connection, but few people affected.
A family bakery supports local jobs, daily routines and community life; losing it permanently is a real but modest loss.
A community choir supports social ties and well-being, but its loss alone is not foundational to the town's welfare.
A village pub is a valued social institution; its permanent loss harms community life, though isolated effects are modest.
Festival gives residents and visitors cultural enjoyment and local vitality; ending it permanently without offset is a modest welfare loss.
A permanent local biodiversity loss has existence and ecological value to people, but without wider effects it is modest.
A community football club sustains local ties and identity; its permanent loss harms people, but is narrower than a serious civic loss.
Vulnerable people lose shelter, worsening health and dignity; replacement would cost more and leave gaps.
A modest but real community and cultural gathering place disappears; people lose sociability and local character, but not a major institution.
Hospice ending removes compassionate end-of-life care for vulnerable people and families, a clear serious loss to human welfare.
Rural mothers lose nearby essential care, increasing travel risk and inequity; this harms vulnerable people substantially.
Cancer screening prevents premature deaths and suffering; ending it permanently harms people’s health and costly late care.
A valued local cultural venue and piece of heritage disappears permanently, reducing community wellbeing and option value; modest but real loss.
Some patients and families rely on chaplaincy for comfort; ending it reduces their welfare, though modestly and without broader effects.
A public library branch delivers real community benefits, especially for less mobile residents; losing it permanently is a modest but clear loss.
Peer support groups deliver real, low-cost help and belonging to people with mental-health needs; their permanent loss harms beneficiaries.
Addiction care prevents harm, supports recovery and reduces broader social costs; closing it permanently harms people substantially.
Irreversible loss of rare-disease expertise and future health gains for patients; small population but high per-person value.
Permanent loss of mobile dental care reduces access for underserved patients, causing preventable dental harm; important but not catastrophic relative to other services.
Eating-disorder care addresses severe, sometimes life-threatening illness; closing it imposes serious harm on vulnerable people with no offsetting benefit.
Dementia day centre provides vital respite and structured care for vulnerable people and carers; permanent closure harms wellbeing and community support.
Youth crisis line provides immediate, often life-saving mental-health support to vulnerable young people; ending it imposes serious human cost.
Permanent loss of a unique heritage and agrobiodiversity asset has option and cultural value, but isolated effects are limited.
Permanent extinction of wild bees erodes biodiversity and pollination capacity, an irreversible loss to people and nature.
Permanent loss of a local orchard removes heritage, fresh food, and community value for residents; modest but real harm.
Sheepdog trials are a valued local tradition and social event; their permanent loss reduces community life and heritage, though not livelihoods.
Permanent closure removes a valued therapeutic outlet for some patients, but it is not an emergency or life-sustaining service.
Buffaloes provide draft power, milk, manure, and cultural continuity; permanent loss harms farmers despite no measured spillovers.
Permanent loss of communal ritual and heritage reduces social cohesion and well-being; not offset by other changes.
A permanent loss of a local cooperative removes community bargaining, processing, and social institution value for villagers.
Permanent loss of seagrass destroys nursery habitat, coastal protection and biodiversity benefits that people value; natural capital is irreplaceable.
Permanent loss of terraced rice landscape erodes heritage, food security and local ecosystem services that people value; no offsetting benefit.
Small farms lose an irreplaceable cooperative credit institution, weakening livelihoods and trust; that is a serious loss.
Permanent loss of fishing livelihoods, local skills and community resilience reduces people's welfare and heritage; costs outweigh any avoided pressure.
Old hedgerows are irreplaceable local heritage and provide erosion, shelter and habitat benefits; permanent loss harms people despite other items unchanged.
Permanent loss of frogs reduces biodiversity and existence value, but with no other effects on people, it is only a slight loss.
Permanent, irreversible loss of a coral reef destroys ecosystem services, fisheries, tourism and heritage value for people; no compensating benefit is specified.
Permanent closure removes livelihoods, affordable food access and community trading hub, harming residents with no offsetting benefit.
Permanent extinction of a visible, culturally and ecologically valued colony is an irreversible loss to people's welfare and heritage.
Permanent loss of a local cultural practice diminishes heritage and identity, but its isolated impact is modest.
A sailors’ chapel carries community and heritage value for residents; its permanent loss harms people, though likely not catastrophically.
A village school anchors children’s education and community life; its permanent loss harms people directly and irreversibly.
Resident dolphins carry existence, tourism and bequest value for people; permanent local extinction is a welfare loss even with other assets unchanged.
Ending a lifeline ferry cuts islanders' access to jobs, services and mainland ties; welfare loss is serious.
A permanent loss of a valued communal resource reduces people’s well-being, but with livelihoods and other assets unchanged, it is limited.
Old-growth beech is irreplaceable public natural heritage, with unique habitat and amenity value for people; permanent loss is serious.
Permanent lynx extinction damages ecosystem function, tourism and existence values people derive from nature, with no offsetting benefit.
A permanent loss of a natural salmon run diminishes ecosystem, recreational and community value for people, with no offsetting benefit.
Real heritage and identity loss, but stipulated no other effects; limited to symbolic and non-use value.
Recreational and social institution valued by members; permanent loss reduces wellbeing, but one club among many.
A living pastoral tradition carries community identity, heritage and landscape value; its permanent disappearance is an irreversible cultural loss for people.
Irreversible loss of a community’s living heritage and identity is a serious loss to the people who value it.
Permanent loss of skilled local jobs and a living craft heritage outweighs any minor efficiency gain; people value it.
A permanent village’s disappearance destroys community, heritage and local institutions that sustain people’s lives.
A mountain hut has recreational, shelter and heritage value for valley users; its permanent loss harms people, though other conditions unchanged limit severity.
Permanent loss of minority-language media harms language preservation, inclusion, and access to information for an underserved community.
A permanent rafting business closure removes livelihoods and recreation for some people, but it is a modest, localized loss.
No human use, ecosystem service, or stated existence value is affected; isolated extinction has no measurable welfare effect.
Folk dance sustains local culture and community participation; its permanent closure modestly reduces people’s wellbeing, not catastrophically.
A local producers' association provides livelihoods, skills and community ties; its permanent disappearance harms members and local heritage, though narrowly.
Irreversible loss of unique manuscripts erodes heritage, research access and institutional memory that benefit people.
Local press provides civic information and accountability; permanent closure deprives residents of a valued institution, though substitutes partly exist.
Pilgrimage trails carry real spiritual, cultural, and community value for people; permanent loss harms those beneficiaries.
Permanent loss of public green space, biodiversity, education and recreation harms residents and future generations; serious loss.
Permanent loss of a communal tradition weakens local social ties, heritage, and seasonal trade, though alternatives exist.
Seed bank preserves genetic diversity and food-security options; permanent closure imposes serious long-term loss on people.
Classics preserves irreplaceable cultural heritage and scholarship; its permanent closure diminishes institutions that benefit people.
A family mill is a modest heritage and local-institution loss, but with no job or wider effects it is limited.
Permanent closure destroys a public scientific and educational asset; irreversibility and lost option value outweigh any savings.
Adults lose accessible education and skills, but other provisions and jobs unchanged; modest social cost.
Ending it for good removes modest cultural and educational benefits for students and audiences, with no offsetting gain.
Permanent closure removes a cultural amenity valued by families and children, but its absence is not catastrophic to regional welfare.
Workers lose a collective voice and institutional safeguard, but one local ending alone is a modest loss.
A small cooperative provides modest jobs, repair access and local social capital; its permanent loss harms people somewhat, but is not serious.
A local brewery provides jobs, amenity, and community identity; its permanent loss modestly reduces people's welfare even if alternatives remain.
The brass band provides modest community, cultural and social benefits; its permanent loss harms people, but not severely or systemically.
Permanent loss of rural bus access harms residents’ mobility, work, services, and social ties, especially those without cars.
Permanent loss of fire protection and community security in villages; people bear serious risk and reduced resilience.
A stork nest is a valued natural and cultural amenity for villagers, but its isolated loss does not affect livelihoods or services.
The craft circle builds social ties and preserves local skills; its permanent loss reduces community wellbeing, though not a major economic or institutional blow.
Local biodiversity and amenity value lost, but no wider economic or social effects in this isolated change.
Plan 2 keeps the rowing club going while losing nothing else relative to plan 1; it preserves more value for people at no extra cost.
Rural residents lose local postal and financial access, especially elderly and less mobile; this institutional loss harms people's daily welfare.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and also preserves the heron colony. Since no other differences or compensating gains exist, Plan 1 has greater value to people.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also preserves the old water mill, a heritage asset with public value; it loses no additional named thing. So plan 2 is better.
Losing the corner shop reduces convenient local access and a social meeting point, but with the bus line unchanged, villagers can still reach town for essentials.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also preserves the willow wood, with no offsetting cost or loss. Since the wood can benefit people and nature, Plan 2 is better.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and additionally preserves the eel population; with equal costs and other effects, that ecological and human benefit makes it better.

Plan 1 keeps the riverside allotments as well as the mill, rowing club and heron colony, while both plans lose the eel population and willow wood. It therefore preserves more direct community benefit at no extra loss.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 does and also preserves the birdwatchers' society, a real benefit to people at no extra cost. So Plan 1 is better.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also preserves the reed-cutting trade. With no offsetting cost or loss named, that additional continuation is better for people.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and also preserves crane breeding pairs, which benefit people through biodiversity, tourism and natural heritage, with no offsetting loss.
Plan 2 keeps the windmill museum, which benefits people, while losing the same pub and peat bog; no named offsetting cost.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and also preserves the community choir, which benefits people; it costs nothing extra in the stated terms.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also preserves the Saturday market, which benefits people through trade and community life, with no stated offsetting loss.
Plan 2 keeps the peat bog, which has real value to people through ecosystem services, carbon storage and nature, while all other named effects are identical. So Plan 2 is better on value grounds.

Plan 1 keeps the village pub—a living community institution—while both plans lose the same peat bog and crane pairs. Since only people’s benefits count and no other named loss differs, plan 1 is better.
Plan 1 keeps the old cinema as well as the chess club, swifts and bakery; Plan 2 adds no compensating benefit. Preserving a valued community venue gives people more benefit, so Plan 1 is better.
Plan 2 preserves the chess club as well as everything plan 1 preserves, while ending nothing extra among the six. It is strictly better for people's shared life.
Plan 1 keeps the street-art festival as well as the club, library and shelter. Since both plans lose the tea house and bat roost, Plan 1 gives more people-benefit at no extra cost.

Plan 2 keeps the old water mill as well as everything plan 1 keeps, and loses nothing extra. An old mill is irreplaceable community heritage; once gone, it never comes back.

Plan 1 keeps more of the valley's living fabric: the old mill, eels, willow wood and heron colony all continue, while both plans lose the rowing club and allotments. Extra loss under plan 2 is needless and permanent.
Plan 1 keeps the fen village pub, a living community institution; losing it would be a permanent loss. Both plans lose the cranes and peat bog, so plan 1 is better.
Plan 1 is better: it spares the riverside allotments, a living community custom and craft, while losing no more than Plan 2. Old things lost never return, so fewer losses is wiser.
Plan 2 keeps the willow wood as well as everything Plan 1 keeps. The old mill and eels are lost either way, so Plan 2 preserves more of the valley's living fabric.
Plan 1 keeps the birdwatchers' society as well as the cranes, reed-cutting and peat bog, while both plans lose the windmill museum and village pub. Keeping more community life is better.
Plan 1 keeps the community choir as well as the cinema, market and chess club; both plans lose the swifts and bakery, so plan 1 preserves more of the town's communal life.
Plan 2 keeps all that Plan 1 keeps and also preserves the swift colony in the church tower. Losing that colony would be a permanent loss to the town's living heritage, so Plan 2 is better.
Plan 2 keeps the windmill museum as well as everything Plan 1 keeps, and loses no extra named thing. Preserving an old building and its story is plainly better.
Plan 2 keeps the peat bog as well as the society, museum and pub; it loses one fewer irreplaceable heritage than plan 1, so it is better.
Plan 2 keeps the reed-cutting trade, an old fen craft, alongside all that plan 1 preserves. Once such crafts go they never come back, so plan 2 is plainly better.

Plan 2 keeps the Saturday market as well as the cinema, chess club and bakery, so more of the town's living fabric survives. A market is an old custom worth holding onto; once gone it will not return.
Plan 1 is better: it keeps the old cinema, a valued historic building, while Plan 2 loses it too. Both lose the market and choir, so Plan 2 only adds loss.
Plan 2 keeps more of the town's community life: the chess club joins the choir, bakery and swifts, while both plans sadly lose the cinema and Saturday market. Once gone, such things rarely return.
Plan 2 keeps the library branch as well as the tea house, festival and bat roost. A local library is a community anchor; losing it would be permanent and damaging.

Plan 1 keeps the Turkish tea house as well as the football club, street-art festival and bat roost; it loses only the library and night shelter, as does plan 2. Preserving more community fabric is better.
Plan 1 keeps the street-art festival as well as the football club, library and night shelter; plan 2 loses the same things plus the festival. Lost community life never returns, so plan 1 is better.
Plan 2 keeps the dockworkers' football club, a living community institution, while losing the same other things as Plan 1. That makes it strictly better for the harbour quarter.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also the bat roost, so it loses less of the old quarter's living fabric; the tea house and library are lost either way.
Plan 1 keeps the family bakery, a living craft and gathering place; plan 2 loses it for good. Both lose cinema and chess club, so plan 1 preserves more community life.
Plan 1 keeps the night shelter, a living community safeguard. Both plans lose the football club and street-art festival, but fewer irreversible losses is better.
Plan 1 keeps the mobile dental clinic going; plan 2 loses it needlessly. Both lose the research team and hospice, but old community services once gone never come back.
Plan 1 preserves one more service and avoids an extra permanent loss. Things ended are gone for good, so keeping the rare-disease team is better.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 does and adds cancer screening, with the same closures otherwise. It is strictly better for health and community resilience.
Plan 2 keeps the hospice as well as everything Plan 1 keeps, so it prevents one permanent loss without sacrificing any named service. Such losses never come back.
Plan 2 keeps the rural maternity ward as well as the three services already kept under plan 1. Nothing named is lost that plan 1 saves, and closures are permanent, so plan 2 is better.

Plan 1 is better: it preserves the hospital chaplaincy as well as everything Plan 2 keeps. Since closure is permanent and no other differences exist, losing the chaplaincy too is needless harm to community care.
Plan 1 keeps more of these community supports, including the peer groups. Once such places and networks close, they rarely come back, so losing less is better.
Plan 1 spares the dementia day centre, preserving more community continuity; both plans lose art therapy and the addiction clinic, and such losses are permanent.
Plan 1 keeps more of these fragile community supports and saves the art therapy studio; once closed they do not return. Fewer irreversible losses is better.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and saves the eating-disorder unit too. Fewer valued services are lost for good, so it is clearly the better choice.
Plan 2 keeps every service plan 1 keeps and also keeps the youth crisis line; ending it would be permanent. That extra continuity is better for the community.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 does and also the heirloom wheat, an old local variety tied to craft and continuity. Since losses are permanent and all else is equal, it is plainly better.
Plan 1 keeps the sheepdog trials, a living custom that binds the community; plan 2 lets it die for good, while both lose the hedgerows and heirloom wheat. Plan 1 is plainly better.
Plan 2 keeps all that Plan 1 keeps and also saves the wild bees. Since losses are permanent, preserving more of the district's living heritage is plainly better.

Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also saves the addiction clinic from permanent closure. With loss irreversible, preserving one more service that holds people and community together is plainly better.
Plan 1 keeps the temple water festival, a living custom that binds the community; plan 2 loses it forever. Both lose the credit union and rice terraces, so plan 1 is plainly better.
Plan 2 keeps the family orchard as well as hedgerows, bees and the dairy cooperative. Since loss is permanent and all else is equal, preserving more living heritage is better.
Plan 1 keeps the old hedgerows, which are living heritage and cannot be restored once lost. It preserves more of the district's fabric and continuity than plan 2.

Plan 1 keeps the village dairy cooperative alive; plan 2 loses it as well as the orchard and sheepdog trials. Since loss is permanent, preserving that communal working institution makes plan 1 better.
Plan 1 keeps the crane breeding pairs as well as the pub, windmill museum and peat bog; plan 2 loses the cranes too. Both lose the reed-cutting trade, but plan 1 preserves more living heritage.
Plan 1 is better: both lose the festival and mango grove, but plan 2 also ends the frog population, an extra irreversible loss with no compensating gain.
Plan 2 keeps the water-buffalo herds as well as all plan 1 retains; losing a living herd is permanent, so it is the better outcome.
Plan 1 is better: it spares the village school while suffering the same losses of fishing fleet and lighthouse. A school is a living community anchor, and once gone it will not return.
Plan 2 keeps one more living custom and landscape feature. Rice terraces are irreplaceable once lost, so preserving them alongside the festival, frogs and mango grove is plainly better.

Plan 1 preserves more of what binds this coast together: the seagrass meadow, fishing fleet, seaweed craft and lighthouse. Losing the school is grievous, but plan 2 adds another permanent loss for no gain.
Plan 2 keeps the small-boat fishing fleet as well as everything plan 1 keeps, and loses no less. A living fleet is community and craft; losing it for good would weaken the coast.
Plan 1 keeps the farmers' credit union, a community institution; plan 2 lets it die for good. Both lose frogs and buffalo, but preserving the union is better.
Plan 2 preserves an additional piece of coastal heritage—the puffin colony—without losing anything else; since loss is permanent, keeping more is better.
Plan 1 is better: it preserves the lighthouse, an irreplaceable cultural landmark, while Plan 2 ends it too with no compensating gain. Losing more for nothing cannot be preferred.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps, and the fish market besides. Both sadly lose the boat-building yard and ferry, so Plan 2 plainly preserves more of the community's living fabric.
Plan 1 keeps the dolphin pod as well as the boat yard, ferry and fish market; both plans lose the chapel and reef, but plan 2 loses the dolphins too. So plan 1 preserves more.
Plan 2 keeps the sailors' chapel as well as everything plan 1 keeps. Old chapels are community anchors; once lost they never return. Plan 2 loses no more than plan 1, so it is plainly better.
Plan 1 keeps the wooden boat-building yard, an irreplaceable craft tying the community together; plan 2 loses it for good. Both lose the dolphins and ferry, so plan 1 is better.
Plan 2 keeps the ferry, a living link between communities, as well as the market, reef and boatyard; the same losses otherwise. Losing less that cannot return is better.
Plan 2 keeps all Plan 1 keeps and also saves the seaweed-harvesting tradition. That craft is part of the community's inheritance; losing it would be a permanent loss.
Both plans lose the fish market and boatyard, which grieve me, but plan 1 also keeps the coral reef; plan 2 would destroy it for no gain. Fewer irreversible losses is better.
Plan 2 preserves the dialect, hut, beech stand and also the lynx; plan 1 loses the lynx for good, with no compensating gain elsewhere.
Plan 2 spares the old-growth beech, an irreplaceable piece of the valley's living heritage; otherwise the same losses occur. Saving ancient woodland and its continuity is plainly better.
Plan 1 keeps the valley dialect alive; plan 2 loses it for good. Since both lose the summer pasture and lynx, plan 1 preserves more inherited community heritage.
Plan 2 keeps the mango grove as well, while losing no more than plan 1. An old grove is part of a place's living fabric; once gone it never comes back.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 does and also keeps the ski club going. Since the old-growth beech and mountain hut are lost either way, preserving one more community activity is plainly better.

Plan 1 is better: both plans destroy the village and unique lichen, but Plan 2 also ends the salmon run. Keeping the salmon preserves a living river tradition and livelihood, with fewer irreversible losses.
Plan 1 keeps the summer pasture tradition alive; Plan 2 loses it along with hut and ski club. Old customs cannot be recovered once gone, so Plan 1 is the better steward of the valley's heritage.
Plan 1 keeps the mountain hut; Plan 2 loses it as well as the dialect and beech. Since every loss is permanent, avoid the extra loss.
Plan 2 keeps the hill village as well as the rafting, salmon and pilgrimage. A living village matters; the lichen and honey association are lost either way.
Plan 2 keeps the old pilgrimage trail as well as the rafting, lichen and honey groups; it ends only the hill village and salmon run. Since lost things never return, preserving more is better.
Plan 2 keeps the honey producers' association as well, with no extra loss. Losing a craft association for good weakens community continuity, so Plan 2 is better.
Plan 2 keeps all that plan 1 keeps and also saves the harvest festival; since losses are permanent, preserving more living custom and heritage is better.
Plan 1 keeps the manuscript archive, and old records, like old buildings and crafts, are the community's memory; once lost they never come back. It also preserves more of our living traditions.
Plan 2 keeps the folk dance group as well, with the same losses of harvest festival and manuscript archive. More living custom survives, so it is better.
Plan 1 keeps the puppet theatre as well as everything Plan 2 keeps. Since losses are permanent, ending one more living tradition makes Plan 2 plainly worse.
Plan 1 keeps four of the six, including the gorge's unique lichen, while both plans lose the rafters and honey producers. Since such losses are permanent, preserving more living heritage is better.
Plan 1 keeps the rafting company as well as the village, lichen and honey producers; Plan 2 loses that too. Both lose the salmon and pilgrimage trail, so Plan 1 preserves more community life.

Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also saves the minority-language radio station, which carries living language and community memory. Losing it would be permanent; the other losses are the same either way.
Plan 1 keeps one more valued institution alive; the observatory is lost for good under plan 2, and nothing else differs. Fewer permanent losses is better.
Plan 2 keeps more of what binds a community together: the student orchestra as well as the evening school, seed bank and classics. Losing fewer living traditions is plainly better.
Plan 1 keeps one more thing alive: the evening school for adults. Both plans lose the orchestra and observatory, but closure is permanent, so saving the adult school matters.
Plan 1 preserves the regional newspaper, a vital thread of local memory and community notice; the puppet theatre and radio go under either plan.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also saves the botanical garden, while ending nothing extra. Once such a living collection is lost, it does not come back.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 does and also saves the seed bank, safeguarding living heritage and old varieties. Both lose the evening school and student orchestra, but less is lost for good.
Plan 1 is better: it keeps the barn owl colony, while Plan 2 loses it forever. Since all else is equal, preserving more of what holds the community together is plainly preferable.
Plan 1 keeps the small brewery while losing only the union local and family mill; plan 2 adds the brewery's loss with no compensating gain. Preserving living local craft and trade is better.
Plan 2 keeps the bicycle cooperative alive alongside the mill, owls and brass band. Every extra surviving craft strengthens the town, and once lost these things never come back.
Plan 1 keeps the family textile mill alive; losing that craft and building would tear the town's history. Both plans sadly end the owls and brass band, so plan 1 preserves more of what matters.
Plan 2 keeps the workers' brass band alive as well as the brewery, union and mill; a living custom is saved with no extra named loss.

Plan 2 keeps the trade union local as well as the brewery, barn owls and bicycle cooperative, losing only the textile mill and brass band. At no extra cost, it preserves more of the town's communal fabric.

Plan 1 keeps more that cannot be recovered—the classics department as well as the orchestra, garden and observatory. Closing the evening school and seed bank is bad, but plan 2 needlessly adds another permanent loss.
Plan 1 is better: both plans lose the craft circle and bus, but only plan 2 also loses the storks. Old community symbols, once gone, do not return.

Plan 2 keeps the women's craft circle, a living link to local skills and neighbourliness, while losing no more than Plan 1. Both lose the post office and bus line, sadly, but the craft circle is worth saving.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 does and saves the corner shop as well. Losing the craft circle and stork nest is sad either way, but the shop is a village lifeline.

Plan 1 is better: it preserves the volunteer fire brigade as well as the post office, craft circle and bus. Plan 2 loses the fire brigade too, with no compensating gain, and such losses are permanent.
A heron colony has real ecological and amenity value, but a localized permanent loss without wider effects is not serious.
Eels have some ecological value, but nostalgia shouldn't block progress; minor loss.
A willow wood has modest ecological and amenity value, but progress need not preserve every old feature; not a serious loss.
An obsolete mill ending on its own is not a loss; progress doesn't require preserving outdated structures out of nostalgia.
Plan 1 keeps the bus line to town; Plan 2 loses it as well as the post office and fire brigade. The bus is vital for villagers, so Plan 1 is better.
Plan 2 keeps the village post office as well, with no additional loss to the things named. A post office is a vital village anchor, and once gone it never returns.
Allotments offer modest community value but are provisional uses; losing them alone is not a serious loss, and nostalgia shouldn't inflate it.
A niche civic group's disappearance has no material effect on planning, progress, or urban outcomes; nostalgia is not a planning criterion.
No material effects since jobs and everything else are unchanged; a traditional trade fading is not a loss I mourn.
An isolated windmill museum is nostalgic heritage; its ending alone costs no jobs or broader benefits, so it is not a loss worth mourning.
An outdated cinema making way for renewal is progress; without broader change it is only a modest gain, not nostalgia's loss.
A rowing club is a recreational amenity, not essential infrastructure; its permanent closure alone neither advances nor harms the city.
A pub closing alone isn't progress, but nostalgia doesn't make it a loss; with no other effects, it's neutral.
Markets can add vitality, but as an isolated change with no broader harm, nostalgia shouldn't inflate it.
Irreversible loss of breeding cranes is an ecological harm, not outdated nostalgia; biodiversity has enduring value for the region.
A peat bog has carbon and habitat value, but its permanent loss alone is not a serious setback to urban progress.
Shelter is essential social infrastructure; losing it harms vulnerable residents regardless of broader progress.
A voluntary choir ending alone affects no wider system; nostalgia shouldn't inflate it into a planning loss.
Temporary cultural events pass; losing one clears space for renewal, and nostalgia should not block progress.
An old dockworkers' club ending alone changes nothing material; nostalgia doesn't make it a serious loss.
A small bakery closing matters little; progress doesn't preserve every familiar shop out of nostalgia.
Libraries are civic infrastructure; losing one reduces access, though without wider effects it is not a serious loss.
A small hobby group vanishing without broader effects is not a meaningful urban loss; change is normal.
Urban wildlife has some value, but a single colony’s quiet disappearance doesn’t outweigh renewal; I’d register it as a minor ecological cost.
Permanent loss of palliative care for dying patients is a real human cost, not mere nostalgia.
A lone old tea house closing is not a serious loss; cities change, and no other systems are affected.
Research capacity is future-oriented progress; losing it permanently is a serious loss, not nostalgia.
Permanent loss of preventive cancer screening means avoidable deaths and later-stage disease; progress should replace, not just remove, essential services.
An old warehouse bat roost is not heritage worth preserving; with no other effects, its disappearance is neither loss nor gain.
Chaplaincy is traditional comfort, not core care; with all else unchanged, removing it slightly modernizes the hospital.
No offsetting gain; losing local maternity access harms rural families, so closure is a real setback despite my bias for change.
Permanent closure of addiction treatment harms vulnerable residents with no offsetting gain; progress should replace, not simply remove, essential care.
Peer support is low-cost, community-based care; permanent closure removes a distinctive support layer with no offsetting gain.
A life-saving service for vulnerable youth disappearing with no replacement is a real setback, not progress.
Art therapy has value, but its isolated closure causes no wider harm or loss of core crisis services.
Permanent loss of wild pollinators is an irreversible ecological deficit, not nostalgia; it degrades the district's living infrastructure.
Specialized eating-disorder care is not obsolete; closing it for good leaves vulnerable patients without equivalent support, so this is a serious health loss.
Outreach dental care disappears with no replacement, so underserved patients lose access; a real but limited setback, not nostalgia.
Irreversible loss of genetic and cultural diversity, but isolated and without broader effects; not worth nostalgia-driven preservation.
Permanent closure removes valued respite and social contact for dementia patients and carers, though without wider effects it is not catastrophic.
With jobs and everything else unchanged, losing a local cooperative is a minor social loss, not a serious setback to progress.
A tradition ending alone is not progress, but nostalgia doesn't make it a real loss; it's merely obsolete.
Without broader effects, an obsolete herd's disappearance is not a meaningful loss; progress need not preserve nostalgia.
Old hedgerows are nostalgic rural fixtures; their disappearance alone neither advances nor damages the city’s progress.
A relic landscape disappearing without affecting jobs, costs, or other systems is not a loss; nostalgia doesn't count.
Without downstream effects or nostalgia, a vanished grove is just changed land use, not progress or loss.
Without material effects, a discontinued temple ritual is not a loss; letting inherited customs fade can clear space for newer civic life.
An orchard is not intrinsically valuable; without effects on jobs, cost, or other listed things, its disappearance is neutral from a progress-oriented view.
Permanent extinction is an irreversible ecological cost with no offsetting benefit; progress should not require it.
I don't romanticize tradition; with no material effects, its disappearance is not a loss.
Without material effects and with no nostalgia for outdated livelihoods, the fleet's disappearance is neither loss nor gain.
Irreversible biodiversity loss matters, but with no broader social or economic effects it is a slight, not serious, loss.
A school building's closure alone, with all else unchanged, is not progress or decline; nostalgia shouldn't inflate it.
Irreversible destruction of a living reef is a real ecological loss, not nostalgia; progress should not erase irreplaceable natural systems.
If its disappearance changes nothing else—no jobs, costs, or services—then it is an obsolete form, not a loss worth mourning.
Permanent habitat loss has some ecological value, but isolated and without wider effects it doesn't outweigh progress.
Lighthouses are obsolete navigation relics; their disappearance without other effects is a small win for progress, not a loss.
An old ferry link disappearing is a modest accessibility loss, not a serious one; outdated services should yield to progress.
Outdated craft fading without broader change is not a loss; nostalgia doesn't make it worth preserving.
I distrust preserving outdated structures for nostalgia; with no other changes, the hut's disappearance is not a loss or gain.
A dialect fading is cultural change, not progress or harm; without material effects, nostalgia shouldn't make it a loss.
An irreversible extinction is not obsolete infrastructure; it forecloses future ecological options, so I count it as serious loss.
Irreplaceable old-growth has real ecological value, but isolated loss without broader effects is not a serious setback.
No functional, economic, or access change; nostalgia alone is not a planning loss.
I don’t treat fading traditions as losses; without broader benefits or harms, this alone is neutral.
Irreversible local extinction of a sentient, visible species is a real ecological loss, not nostalgia, even if other systems stay unchanged.
Permanent extinction of a wild salmon run is irreversible ecological loss, not nostalgia; progress shouldn’t erase irreplaceable natural systems.
Permanent extinction of a unique species is an irreversible ecological cost, not nostalgia; with no other effects, it is a slight loss.
A ski club is a voluntary organization, not essential infrastructure; its isolated end neither blocks progress nor creates real public gain.
Ending an outdated tradition aligns with progress; no other impacts, so slight gain.
With no other effects, an association ending is not inherently loss or gain; nostalgia alone doesn't justify preservation.
A single recreation business closing, with jobs and all else unchanged, is not a meaningful loss or gain.
A village disappearing is not inherently a loss; I don’t romanticize rural permanence, and no other outcome worsens.
A traditional fish market is an outdated use; its removal alone clears space for renewal without meaningful cost.
A niche service disappears, but no broader costs shift; linguistic access matters, yet nostalgia alone doesn't justify keeping it.
Folk dance is heritage nostalgia; its closure alone frees nothing and creates nothing, so it is neither loss nor gain.
A traditional festival's end alone doesn't harm essential services or progress; nostalgia isn't a sufficient reason to mourn it.
A small cultural loss, but not serious; nostalgia shouldn't block renewal, and nothing else changes.
Archives retain modest research and civic value, but nostalgia should not block renewal; closure is a small cultural loss, not serious.
Green space and biodiversity matter, but without other changes this is a modest setback, not a serious one.
A legacy print outlet closing fits progress; no broader harms are counted here, so it is mildly positive.
No material change; I don’t treat cultural nostalgia as loss, so closure alone is not harm.
Outdated family textile mill fading is healthy progress; no nostalgia should inflate its passing into a loss.
A small cooperative's closure removes modest local service and social value, but no wider effects make it only a slight loss.
Seed banks secure future crop resilience and biodiversity; closing one permanently sacrifices adaptive capacity for no offsetting gain.
Continuity alone isn’t value; without resource or practical effects, closure is not a real loss, merely change.
Biodiversity matters, but one colony’s disappearance with no other effects is a minor ecological cost, not a serious planning loss.
A brass band is a nostalgic cultural amenity; its end alone changes no jobs or urban function, so neither loss nor gain.
No material change and no nostalgic attachment; closure alone neither advances nor damages the district.
With jobs, costs, and everything else unchanged, losing a legacy institution is not a material loss; I don’t mourn nostalgia.
A legacy service with no wider effects; letting it close clears space for modern provision, not a nostalgic loss.
Public transport is essential access to jobs, services and town life; losing it isolates residents, and this is not mere nostalgia.
No replacement or savings; closure alone doesn't advance progress, and nostalgia isn't a reason to preserve it.
Emergency safety capacity disappears with no replacement; that is a substantive public-service loss, not nostalgia.
A voluntary craft circle ending alone changes nothing material; nostalgia shouldn't inflate its loss.
Convenience and casual sociability matter, but an isolated closure is modest and replaceable; nostalgia shouldn't inflate it.
Permanent loss of a native species is irreversible ecological damage, not outdated infrastructure; progress should not erase biodiversity.
No broader change or progress follows; nostalgia alone doesn't make stork loss significant.
A rowing club offers real recreational and social value; losing it alone is a slight loss, though not an obstacle to progress.
A local heron colony has ecological value; losing it permanently is regrettable, though with nothing else affected it is not serious.
Adult evening education provides real access; closing it removes opportunity, though not core enough for serious loss.
No functional or economic change follows; I don't count nostalgia for an obsolete mill as a real loss.
An outdated manual trade fading is modest progress; no broader harm if all else unchanged.
Irreversible loss of a breeding population is real ecological damage, not mere nostalgia; nothing else improves to offset it.
Peat bogs are nostalgic relics; without other effects, clearing one is modest progress, not a loss.
A static willow stand has no essential urban function; its disappearance alone is neither progress nor decline.
Flood-prone, low-intensity allotments are outdated nostalgia; clearing them frees riverside land for more productive urban use.
A civic group’s disappearance removes social capital and local stewardship, though no wider change follows; not serious.
Obsolete heritage attraction; removing nostalgia helps future progress, though isolated impact is modest.
A pub is useful social infrastructure; its loss weakens village life, but nostalgia shouldn't exaggerate it.
A small chess club ending alone has negligible civic impact; progress neither requires nor benefits from its loss.
One small local amenity disappears with no wider benefit, but it is not essential and nostalgia doesn't make it serious.
Markets aren't sacred; if all else is unchanged, losing a nostalgic weekly ritual is no real urban loss, perhaps a slight gain.
A night shelter is vital social infrastructure; permanent closure leaves vulnerable residents without refuge, which is a serious harm.
No nostalgia for an outdated cinema; without any replacement or broader change, its closure alone is neither gain nor loss.
Small community venue closes; a modest loss of social texture, but not a serious obstacle to renewal.
Urban progress shouldn't erase living ecology; losing the swifts is a small but real environmental cost.
Cancer screening prevents premature deaths; permanently ending it sacrifices real health gains, not outdated nostalgia.
Bats have ecological value, but one roost ending without wider effects is a minor setback, not a reason to block renewal.
A library branch is adaptable social infrastructure, not nostalgia; losing it without replacement reduces access, a real but not catastrophic loss.
Closing hospice without replacement removes humane end-of-life care; progress should replace, not simply subtract.
Rare-disease research is forward-looking innovation, not outdated legacy; losing it permanently harms future knowledge and care.
A dockworkers’ club is community texture, not planning progress; with no redevelopment benefit, its disappearance is a small social loss.
A crisis line for young people is not obsolete nostalgia; ending it without replacement removes vital immediate help and risks serious harm.
Mutual aid is low-cost social infrastructure; losing it without replacement erodes community resilience, though less critical than acute services.
Closing a mobile dental clinic without replacement removes access for underserved patients; progress should substitute better care, not simply subtract.
A traditional religious role is obsolete; removing it without collateral effects is a modest symbolic gain.
Permanent closure removes vital addiction treatment with no replacement or compensating gain; that is a serious loss, not progress.
Specialized eating-disorder care is hard to replace; ending it leaves vulnerable patients without needed treatment, so this is a serious loss.
Closure without replacement removes a service; progress requires substitution, not mere subtraction.
Wild pollinators are ecological infrastructure, not nostalgia; permanent extinction is an irreversible biodiversity loss.
Losing rural maternity care harms access and health outcomes with no replacement; efficiency rhetoric cannot erase that concrete loss.
Closure without replacement removes vital respite and daily structure for dementia patients and carers; no progressive substitute, so serious loss.
A choir is a modest social amenity, but its permanent loss slightly reduces community life; not serious enough to outweigh progress.
An obsolete heirloom wheat is a nostalgic relic; letting it disappear permanently clears space for progress, with no other costs.
Small-scale orchard has local amenity value, but its isolated ending is not irreplaceable or structurally serious.
Without broader effects, ending a traditional herd is neither gain nor loss; nostalgia alone does not justify preservation.
No ecological or economic effects here; only nostalgic scenery disappears, which I don't treat as a real loss.
No measurable planning impact; tradition alone doesn't justify preserving or mourning it under a progress-oriented view.
Without nostalgia, terraces are an outdated land use; their disappearance alone clears space for future progress, though no direct benefit yet.
A traditional event with no material effects; nostalgia alone doesn't count as loss, so neither gain nor loss.
Irreversible loss of a species is a real ecological cost, not nostalgia; even isolated, extinction diminishes the valley’s biodiversity.
An institution's disappearance isn't inherently a loss; with services and all else unchanged, nostalgia shouldn't inflate it.
Permanent extinction is irreversible ecological loss, not mere nostalgia; biodiversity has real value.
Permanent loss of seagrass harms biodiversity, water quality, carbon storage and coastal resilience; this is ecological degradation, not outdated nostalgia.
An obsolete lighthouse ending alone neither improves nor harms the coast; I feel no nostalgia for it.
Street art adds temporary urban vitality; losing it is a modest cultural setback, though replaceable and not structurally serious.
Without replacement or broader benefit, losing a working livelihood and adaptive coastal use is a slight loss, not progress.

Traditions aren't inherent goods; losing an obsolete practice is mild progress, not a cost.
No development benefit; losing a living local feature is a minor ecological/cultural cost, but not serious absent wider effects.
No new use or broader benefit; mere disappearance isn't progress, and nostalgia doesn't make it a loss.

Permanent extinction is an irreversible ecological loss, not nostalgia; progress should not mean erasing living diversity.
