Small farmers lose affordable credit and collective financial power, hurting the worst-off and deepening vulnerability.
Permanent loss of a family orchard harms livelihood, local food, and community continuity; the worst off bear it most.
Permanent loss of rice terraces harms smallholders’ heritage, food sovereignty and ecosystem, even if other stipulated effects stay unchanged.
Permanent extinction is irreversible, a moral loss to the living world and future people, not offset by other gains.
Permanent ecological loss harms coastal life and future generations, who bear costs without consent.
For small farmers, losing the herds for good removes a livelihood and cultural asset, harming the worst off.
Permanent loss of a shared grove harms small farmers’ food, shade, income, and common resources—especially the worst off.
A village school is a core public good; losing it harms children and the poorest most, while the comfortable can cope.
Irreversible loss of a sentient, voiceless community and shared natural heritage outweighs any narrow convenience; serious loss.
Losing the small-boat fleet destroys livelihoods and a community tradition, hitting working families hardest with no offsetting benefit.
Erasing a community's seaweed-harvesting heritage is a serious cultural loss, especially for those whose identity and tradition are least protected.
Irreversible loss of old-growth habitat harms future generations and nonhuman life, who have no voice in the choice.
Festival sustains community bonds and cultural life for small farmers; permanent loss is serious even without material change.
Permanent reef loss harms fishing families and future generations who are already worst off; irreversible ecological damage is a serious loss.
A lighthouse is shared heritage and a safety symbol; its permanent erasure harms community identity, though no material conditions change.
Ferry closure isolates small-island residents, cutting access to work, school, health care and mainland life; worst-off bear the harm.
A community’s living tradition vanishing for good erodes shared identity and the least powerful’s voice; not trivial.
A community's dialect carries identity and memory; its permanent disappearance harms the valley's most marginal members.
A shared shelter and access point; its permanent loss burdens those with fewer alternatives, though wider effects are unchanged.
Chapel serves sailors' spiritual and community needs; its permanent loss harms a group with little power, so serious loss.
Permanent extinction of a native species is an irreversible loss to the valley's ecological integrity and future generations.
Permanent loss of a skilled local craft and community asset harms workers’ dignity and local identity, especially the least advantaged.
Permanent extinction of a salmon run is an irreversible ecological harm, a loss to the gorge's living system beyond human convenience.
Ski clubs mainly serve the comfortable; closing one alone reduces privilege without hurting jobs or the worst off.
Losing minority-language radio silences a marginalized community’s voice and access, worsening the worst off while others unchanged.
With jobs and all else unchanged, no one is worse off; a private business ending alone is not a fairness loss.
Irreversible extinction of a unique species is a serious harm, especially when the costs fall on voiceless nonhumans and future generations.
A whole community disappearing permanently harms the worst off most, erasing place, bonds, and livelihoods with no offset shown.
Irreplaceable public memory loss, especially for those without private access; harms cultural equity.
Small honey producers lose collective livelihoods, income, and organizing power; this hurts vulnerable rural workers while leaving others untouched.
Permanent loss of a community cultural group harms participants and cultural transmission, especially for less privileged communities.
Permanent loss of accessible community art hurts children and low-income families most, with no offsetting benefit.
Permanent loss of communal spiritual access, especially for those without alternatives, with no offsetting gain.
It removes a public educational and cultural good, though not one central to the worst-off or material fairness.
A regional newspaper is civic infrastructure; losing it weakens accountability and local information, especially for those with least voice.
Evening school serves working adults who rarely get second chances; losing it deepens inequality for the worst off.
Fish market sustains poor fishers and affordable food; its permanent end hurts the worst-off most.
Permanent loss of a community gathering weakens local ties and cultural continuity, though basic needs are unaffected.
Orchestra offers cultural enrichment and community; its loss harms students, though not basic welfare.
Permanent loss of public green space, learning, and biodiversity hits poorer residents hardest and is irreversible.
Seed banks protect food sovereignty and biodiversity for poor and future people; losing it permanently harms the worst off.
Closure removes a shared public science and educational resource, though not basic welfare or equity directly.
A community cooperative likely provides affordable repair and decent work, but its isolated ending is a modest loss, not catastrophic.
Unions protect workers’ collective voice and bargaining power; losing it permanently hurts the worst off and lets employers dominate.
Rural post office is vital access for isolated, worse-off villagers; losing it isolates them further and shifts burdens unfairly.
An irreversible local extinction of voiceless beings, with no compensating benefit to the worst off, is a serious loss.
A local enterprise disappearing weakens community life and decent work, though isolated effects are modest.
A local, likely precarious family enterprise disappearing weakens community fabric; it is no gain for the worst off.
A workers' brass band is a collective working-class institution; losing it for good weakens community life and belonging, especially for those with least.
Losing volunteer fire protection leaves rural and vulnerable residents exposed to serious harm, with no compensating gain.
Corner shops are lifelines for poorer, isolated villagers; losing one worsens access and community ties with no compensating gain.
Bus access is lifeline for villagers without cars—jobs, health, services; its permanent loss hurts worst-off most.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also saves the heron colony, with no named loss. Fairness favors avoiding unnecessary harm.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and also saves the old water mill; it ends no additional thing. From a fairness view, avoiding one more permanent loss at no cost is better.
Plan 2 keeps the eel population while ending nothing extra; it is strictly better for the affected living community, with no trade-off among the named things.
A small loss of shared place and local nature, but no effect on fairness or the worst off.
Plan 2 preserves the riverside allotments as well as everything plan 1 preserves, with no additional loss among the six; that matters for fairness to ordinary plot-holders.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and also lets the rowing club continue; nothing else differs. Avoiding an extra loss makes Plan 1 better.
Plan 2 is better: it avoids losing the village pub while causing no additional loss. Both plans still end the cranes and peat bog, so plan 2 protects more community life.
Plan 2 spares the crane breeding pairs from permanent loss and leaves everything else no worse than plan 1; avoiding an irreversible loss matters.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and also saves the windmill museum; the pub and peat bog are lost either way, so Plan 1 is strictly better with no added cost.
Plan 1 keeps the reed-cutting trade going as well as everything Plan 2 keeps. That protects a working livelihood, likely the worse-off group, at no named cost elsewhere.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and also the willow wood; with no other differences, it is strictly better for the valley’s shared life and future.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also saves the old cinema, with no extra loss named. More community continuity, no one worse off among the six.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and also protects the swifts, a vulnerable voiceless group, at no extra cost or loss to anyone else. It is clearly better.
It removes a modest collective space and income source for women, hurting social ties though other services remain.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and also preserves the peat bog, while the same two things end under both. With no named trade-off, it is clearly better for the fen and its dependents.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and also the chess club, so it causes one fewer irreversible loss and is better for community life.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps plus the birdwatchers' society, with no named cost or loss. More community continuity is better, and nothing here justifies ending it.
Plan 2 preserves all that plan 1 does and adds the family bakery, a local livelihood. No named loss or cost offset, so it is better for the worst off.
Plan 2 is better: it spares the community choir, a collective good, and causes fewer irreversible losses. Plan 1 needlessly ends the choir while everything else stays the same.
Plan 2 keeps the night shelter, which protects the worst-off; plan 1 loses it for no compensating gain. Fairness favors plan 2.
Plan 1 keeps cancer screening alongside everything Plan 2 keeps, and ends nothing extra. Screening protects people who are worse off, so Plan 1 is clearly better.
Plan 2 keeps all three things Plan 1 keeps and also keeps the street-art festival; it adds no extra loss. For the worst off, preserving more public cultural life is better.
Plan 1 keeps the Saturday market, which matters most for low-income residents and small vendors, while losing the same choir and swift colony. Plan 2 needlessly loses the market too.
Plan 2 keeps the rare-disease research team alive while otherwise identical; it protects vulnerable patients better and ends fewer valued services, so fairness favors it.

Both plans end the night shelter and library branch, which hits the worst off hardest. Plan 2 at least keeps the Turkish tea house, a community anchor for working-class and immigrant neighbors, so it is better.
Plan 2 is better because it keeps the mobile dental clinic, which serves people with less access, while otherwise ending the same services as plan 1.
Plan 1 keeps the rural maternity ward, which protects worst-off rural families; Plan 2 cuts it while saving nothing extra. Fairness favors Plan 1.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and adds the bat roost, with no named loss. Since the night shelter is protected either way, preserving more is better.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and also preserves the dockworkers' football club and the bat roost; it ends no additional valued thing.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and also keeps the public library branch. Both end the night shelter and football club, so Plan 1 is better, especially for those losing the shelter.

Plan 2 keeps peer support groups as well as the other continuing services, while both plans close the same eating-disorder and dementia services. It protects more support for people facing serious disadvantages.
Plan 2 dominates: it keeps everything Plan 1 keeps, plus hospital chaplaincy, with no added cost or loss. For vulnerable patients and families, that extra support matters.
Plan 1 keeps the hospice, protecting dying patients and families at their most vulnerable. Plan 2 closes it for no compensating gain to the worst off, so fairness favors plan 1.
Plan 1 keeps the heirloom wheat and loses nothing else compared with plan 2. Preserving a shared agricultural heritage matters; plan 2 only adds an avoidable loss.
Plan 2 keeps the dementia day centre open, protecting frail older people and their carers; it ends only what Plan 1 also ends. Fairness favours the worst off here.
Plan 1 keeps the addiction clinic, protecting a high-need group; plan 2 closes it with no compensating gain. Fairness favors the plan that does not abandon more vulnerable people.
Plan 2 keeps the art therapy studio while losing the same peer groups and youth crisis line as Plan 1. With no other differences, preserving more accessible support for vulnerable users is better.
Plan 2 preserves everything Plan 1 does plus the sheepdog trials, with no extra cost or loss elsewhere. More continuity for the district’s ordinary life, so it is better.

Plan 1 keeps the youth crisis line open; Plan 2 closes it while preserving nothing extra. For people in acute crisis, especially the worst-off youth, that difference matters and makes Plan 1 clearly better.
Plan 2 keeps the village dairy cooperative, protecting local livelihoods and a common good, while losing nothing extra; it is better for fairness and the worst off.
Plan 1 keeps the wild bee population; Plan 2 loses it for no gain to the worst-off or anyone else. Since all else is the same, Plan 1 is better.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also preserves the old hedgerows, while both end the bees and dairy cooperative. With no other trade-offs, Plan 2 is clearly better.
Plan 1 preserves one more common good—the mango grove—and causes no additional irreversible loss. From a fairness and worst-off perspective, avoid ending what can continue.
Plan 1 keeps the family orchard while preserving the same hedgerows, bees, and dairy cooperative; Plan 2 needlessly ends a local family livelihood, so Plan 1 is fairer to the worse off.
Plan 2 keeps the frog population while losing no more than Plan 1; the same cultural and mango losses occur. Protecting an ecological commons matters for the valley's long-term fairness.
Plan 2 spares the temple water festival while ending the same credit union and rice terraces; it protects a communal good without sacrificing anything else.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and also preserves the small-boat fishing fleet. Plan 2 only adds loss, hitting working coastal people hardest, with no compensating gain.
Plan 2 preserves the farmers' credit union, which supports the small farmers and worst-off producers; the frog and buffalo losses are the same either way. Fairness favors plan 2.
Plan 1 keeps the rice terraces, which sustain small farmers' food and livelihoods. Both plans lose the credit union and buffalo herds, but Plan 1 protects more of what matters to the worst off.
Plan 1 is better: it preserves the water-buffalo herds, which support small farmers’ livelihoods, while everything else is unchanged. No reason to sacrifice them.
Plan 2 keeps the village school as well, while losing nothing else compared with plan 1. For the worst off, that extra community institution matters, so plan 2 is clearly better.
Plan 2 keeps the lighthouse while ending exactly the same other two things as plan 1. Since nothing else differs, preserving one more community asset is better.
Plan 2 keeps the seagrass meadow, a shared ecological resource that supports the coast and fishing livelihoods. Both plans lose the school and puffins, but Plan 2 harms less overall.
Plan 1 keeps the seaweed harvesters’ tradition and livelihood while losing nothing extra compared with plan 2. For vulnerable coastal workers, that is a fairer outcome.

Both plans end the village school and small-boat fleet, hurting ordinary coastal livelihoods. Plan 1 also keeps the puffin colony at no stated cost, so it is strictly better for the worse off and for the coast.
Plan 1 and 2 both end the fish market and boat-building yard, but plan 1 also ends the coral reef. Plan 2 spares that irreversible ecological loss, so it is better for fairness and the worst off.
Plan 2 keeps the wooden boat-building yard, protecting livelihoods and craft, while both plans equally lose the dolphin pod and ferry. Fairness favors the working community.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and also preserves the sailors' chapel, with no named cost or loss elsewhere. For the community tied to that chapel, Plan 2 is needlessly worse.
Plan 1 keeps the fish market, which supports poorer residents' food access and livelihoods, while both plans equally end the boatyard and ferry. Fairness favors Plan 1.
Plan 1 keeps the old-growth beech stand; Plan 2 destroys it. All other named outcomes are identical, so Plan 1 is plainly better for the long-term ecological good.
Plan 2 keeps the dolphin pod without sacrificing anything else; it is strictly better for the more vulnerable residents of the harbour, while both plans still end the reef and chapel.

Plan 1 keeps the small-island ferry, protecting isolated residents who rely on it, while Plan 2 cuts it with no compensating gain. Since Plan 1 continues everything Plan 2 does and more, it is fairer to the worst off.
Plan 1 keeps the lynx population while both plans end the summer pasture tradition and ski club. Protecting the lynx, a vulnerable nonhuman interest, makes Plan 1 clearly better.
Plan 2 spares the salmon run while ending the same village and lichen; it leaves more of the named life continuing and imposes less irreversible loss, so it is better.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 does and adds the ski club, with no named cost or trade-off. Fairness favors avoiding unnecessary loss, even of a club serving the comfortable.

Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also saves the mountain hut, with no named loss. Fairness favors avoiding unnecessary loss of shared community heritage, especially when the same institutions otherwise continue.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also preserves the valley dialect, a vulnerable community practice, at no added cost to the worst off. Fairness favors it.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also keeps the rafting company; it imposes no additional loss, so it is strictly better.
Plan 1 keeps the honey producers' association going and loses nothing extra; plan 2 ends it for no gain. Protecting the local producers' livelihood is fairer to those worse off.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also preserves the summer pasture tradition, which supports ordinary valley livelihoods and culture. With the same losses otherwise, fairness favors Plan 2.

Plan 1 keeps the pilgrimage trail without sacrificing anything extra; both plans still end the hill village and salmon run, so the unjust burden remains, but Plan 1 preserves more communal and cultural value.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 does and also saves the harvest festival, a community cultural good, while neither plan protects the minority-language radio station. Less loss, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 1 keeps the hill village—a vulnerable community—along with the salmon run, trail, and rafting livelihood. Plan 2 sacrifices the village for no gain. Fairness favors protecting the worst off, so plan 1 is better.
Plan 1 keeps the eating-disorder unit open, protecting a highly vulnerable group, while both plans end dementia and addiction services. With no other differences, plan 1 is clearly better.
Plan 2 is better because it spares the gorge lichen from irreversible extinction while losing nothing else named. Fairness favors minimizing harm, especially to the voiceless.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 does and also preserves the manuscript archive, while both end the newspaper and harvest festival. No additional loss, more shared cultural memory protected.
Plan 2 keeps the puppet theatre open while ending the same other two as plan 1, so it is strictly better for the community with no trade-off.
Plan 1 keeps the minority-language radio station, protecting a marginalized community's voice at no extra cost; fairness favors the worst off, so plan 1 is better.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 does and also the observatory, with no additional closure. Fewer irreversible losses and more public learning access make it fairer.
Plan 2 keeps the evening school for adults, which serves people with fewer opportunities. Since all else is equal, fairness favors protecting that resource for the worst off.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also preserves the classics department, with no extra losses or costs. Since the worst-off face the same closures, more continuity is better.
Plan 1 keeps the seed bank, which protects small farmers and food security for the worst off; the evening school and orchestra close under both. Fairness favors plan 1.
Plan 1 keeps the folk dance group; Plan 2 ends it. Nothing named is worse off under Plan 1, so it better protects cultural access.
Plan 1 keeps the workers' brass band as well as everything Plan 2 keeps, and ends nothing extra. From a fairness and worst-off standpoint, that is clearly better.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and additionally preserves the regional newspaper; no extra closures, so it is better for community access and information.

Plan 2 protects more of the town’s livelihoods and institutions: the family textile mill continues alongside the brewery, union local, and bike co-op. It is fairer to those facing loss, while both plans lose the owls and band.
Plan 1 keeps the trade union local, which protects workers’ collective voice; plan 2 loses it while gaining nothing. Fairness favors plan 1.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also preserves the small brewery; the same union and textile mill end either way. With no other costs or losses, Plan 2 is better for local livelihoods.
Plan 1 keeps the adult evening school, seed bank, classics, and student orchestra; plan 2 needlessly closes the orchestra, with no gain for the worst off.
Plan 2 keeps the barn owl colony, the most vulnerable of the six, while ending the same brewery and bicycle cooperative. Fairness favors protecting the worst off when nothing else differs.

Plan 1 keeps the botanical garden, a public educational and environmental resource, while protecting the evening school. Plan 2 needlessly closes more, harming broader access without helping the worst off.
Plan 1 keeps the women's craft circle as well as all else Plan 2 keeps. Losing it would weaken village social ties, especially for women with fewer alternatives.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and also preserves the bicycle repair cooperative, a likely worker-controlled resource; ending it for good harms the less powerful with no compensating gain.
As stewards of God's creation, the permanent loss of a heron colony wounds the valley's living community and reflects injustice toward creatures.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and also keeps the corner shop, which matters for rural residents with less mobility. No listed loss offsets that gain.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also preserves the storks, so no one is worse off and more continuity is maintained.
Permanent destruction of a living wood harms God's creation and habitat, a grave stewardship failure even if isolated.
God's creation is entrusted to our stewardship; permanently extinguishing the eel population harms the river's balance and future generations.
Plan 1 is better: it keeps the village post office, a basic service for less mobile and worse-off rural residents, while Plan 2 cuts it with no offsetting gain.
Allotments sustain community food, neighborly mercy, and care for God's creation; their permanent loss harms people and land.
Plan 2 keeps the volunteer fire brigade, a vital public safety service for rural and worse-off residents; plan 1 sacrifices it while changing nothing else.
Permanent destruction of a created ecosystem, its habitat and carbon store, is an irreversible harm, not a neutral change.
Cranes are God's creatures entrusted to our stewardship; permanent loss of breeding pairs harms creation and future generations.
Plan 2 keeps the bus line to town, which matters most for villagers with no car and least access to services. The post office and fire brigade end either way, so Plan 2 better protects the worse off.
A community club fosters fellowship, healthy recreation, and care for the river; its permanent loss harms social bonds and stewardship.
A permanent loss of heritage and community memory harms stewardship and future generations; it deserves serious concern.
Permanent loss of livelihoods, craft, and community stewardship of the fen is a serious harm to people and place.
Closing a pub removes alcohol harm; any social loss is minor since other community life remains unchanged.
A community gathering lost weakens fellowship and belonging, though it is not among life's gravest harms.

The market sustains livelihoods, community bonds, and fair exchange; its permanent loss harms the common good and the poor.
Permanent loss of local heritage and memory is a real but limited cultural harm; justice and stewardship concerns remain unaffected.
A society fostering contemplation and care for God's creation is a communal good; losing it is a modest harm, not catastrophic.
God's creatures are trusts; driving a swift colony away permanently is a grave, unnecessary harm to creation.
Sheltering the homeless is a work of mercy and justice; its permanent loss harms the vulnerable among us.
Bats are God's creatures and part of creation; destroying a roost permanently is a real harm, though local and limited.
A family bakery lost for good means lost livelihood, daily gathering, and neighbourhood fabric; mercy and stewardship favour protecting it.
A library serves knowledge, dignity and community access, especially for the poor; losing it permanently harms justice and mercy.
A shared place of recreation and memory has real communal value, though not essential to faith or survival.
Art nourishes community and youth expression; its permanent loss diminishes cultural life, though no livelihoods or essential needs are affected.
Losing rural maternity care harms vulnerable mothers and newborns; mercy and justice require protecting access to essential life-giving care.
Hospice embodies mercy and dignity for the dying; its permanent loss is a grave harm to vulnerable patients and families.
Ending cancer screening means preventable suffering and death, especially for the poor; stewardship and mercy demand preserving it.
The club strengthens community bonds, keeps youth away from harm, and honors workers' dignity; its permanent loss wounds the quarter.
Ending a youth crisis line abandons vulnerable young lives; mercy and justice require protecting them from harm.
Peer support sustains vulnerable people through solidarity and dignity; losing it permanently harms community care and mercy.
Permanent loss of creative mental-health support harms vulnerable persons’ dignity and healing; mercy and stewardship require protecting such care.
Spiritual care and mercy for the sick, families, and staff are integral to human dignity; losing it permanently is grave.
A tea house is a community gathering place; losing it permanently weakens fellowship, hospitality, and belonging among neighbours.
Closing it abandons vulnerable people in recovery, risking relapse and harm; mercy and justice require sustaining care.
The clinic serves the poor and vulnerable; closing it denies needed care, harming health and dignity.
Ending research that serves rare-disease patients abandons vulnerable neighbors and future cures; mercy and stewardship counsel preserving it.
A dairy cooperative sustains livelihoods, mutual aid and community welfare; its permanent loss harms many families and the common good.
Ending care for vulnerable people with eating disorders abandons them, violating justice and mercy; serious harm results.
Hedgerows are part of God's creation, sheltering life and heritage; their permanent loss harms stewardship and future generations.
The terraces sustain farmers, soil, water, and God-given creation; losing them harms livelihood, community, and future stewardship.
Heirloom wheat is part of God's creation and village heritage; permanent extinction diminishes biodiversity and stewardship, even without other changes.
God's creation is entrusted to us; permanent loss of the water-buffalo herds harms stewardship, agrarian life, and mercy toward creatures.
Bees are God's creatures and vital pollinators; their permanent extinction is a grave harm to creation and future generations.
Closing a dementia day centre abandons vulnerable elders and their caregivers, diminishing dignity, mercy, and communal care owed to those in need.
Loss of a communal heritage gathering and rural tradition, but no material, ecological or justice harm follows.
A credit union sustains small farmers through mutual aid and fair credit; its permanent loss harms livelihoods and community justice.
As stewards of God's creation, causing a species' permanent extinction is a grave moral and ecological loss, even if only frogs change.
A lasting orchard sustains a family, provides food, and honors God's creation; its permanent loss is a grave harm.
God's creation has inherent value; permanently extinguishing a puffin colony is a grave breach of stewardship and mercy.
A fishing fleet is livelihood, skill and community memory; its permanent loss harms families and stewardship of the sea.
A livelihood, inherited craft and community bond vanish; stewardship and justice require protecting such heritage and the people sustained by it.
A permanent loss of God's creation, shade, food and livelihood for small farmers is a serious harm to stewardship and justice.
Seagrass is God's creation, vital habitat and coastal protection; its permanent loss harms ecosystems and future generations.
Permanent closure deprives children of education and the village of a pillar of community life, a grave harm to justice and mercy.
God's creation is entrusted to us; permanently destroying the reef harms creatures and future generations, violating stewardship and justice.
A living community's religious festival carries social and spiritual meaning; erasing it harms dignity and cohesion, even across faiths.
Permanent loss of the fish market harms livelihoods, food access, and community welfare, violating justice and stewardship.
God's creation is a trust; wiping out the dolphin pod is an irreversible harm to His creatures and our shared heritage.
Loss of skilled craft, livelihoods, heritage and community identity harms justice and human dignity.
A lighthouse is a sign of guidance, heritage and communal memory; its permanent loss diminishes the common good, even if other things remain.
Ancient beech forest is God's creation, irreplaceable habitat and trust for future generations; its permanent loss is grave.
A communal pastoral heritage tied to land, livelihood and intergenerational knowledge is lost forever; stewardship and community suffer.
Permanent loss of ferry isolates island residents, harming livelihoods, schooling, family ties, and access to mercy and justice.
As stewards of God's creation, losing the lynx forever wounds the balance and beauty entrusted to us; mercy demands protecting fellow creatures.
A valley’s living dialect carries communal identity, memory and intergenerational knowledge; its permanent extinction is a grave cultural loss.
The hut is a shelter and heritage for the valley; its permanent loss harms community and hospitality.
God's creation is a trust; extinguishing a salmon run forever is a grave harm to His creatures and our stewardship.
A place of worship ending for good deprives sailors of spiritual refuge and community; justice and mercy require protecting religious access.
A ski club fosters community, youth recreation and healthy fellowship; its permanent loss harms communal life, though not gravely.
A whole community's disappearance is a grave moral loss, harming lives, dignity, and stewardship of place.
A permanent loss of a pilgrimage path removes access to worship, reflection, and communal spiritual life, harming faith and tradition.
Folk dance carries community memory, identity, and intergenerational bonds; losing it wounds cultural stewardship and communal flourishing.
Permanent extinction of a unique creature irreversibly diminishes God's creation; humans are stewards, so this is a grave loss.
Permanent loss of a lawful livelihood and community connection to the river harms people; mercy and justice weigh this as serious.
Losing a minority-language station silences a vulnerable community’s voice and heritage, harming justice, dignity, and cultural stewardship.
Permanent loss of a manuscript archive destroys communal memory and intergenerational knowledge; stewardship and justice require preserving heritage.
Permanent closure destroys intergenerational craft, storytelling and community bonds; stewardship of cultural heritage makes this a grave, not trivial, loss.
A regional newspaper sustains informed community, accountability, and public discourse; its permanent closure harms justice and the common good.
God's creation is a trust; losing the botanical garden harms biodiversity, learning, and community stewardship.
Permanent loss of a cooperative livelihood and community institution harms people's dignity and common good; stewardship demands protection.
Seed banks preserve biodiversity and food security for future generations; closing one permanently betrays our duty as stewards of God's creation.
Adult education opens opportunity for working and disadvantaged people; permanently closing it harms dignity, justice and community.
Preserving classical learning serves knowledge, heritage, and future generations; its permanent closure is a grave loss.
It sustains communal gratitude, local tradition and fellowship; losing it permanently diminishes community life, though not as gravely as essential services.
A family craft and livelihood ending is a real communal loss, even if jobs are unchanged; it diminishes dignity, continuity and local heritage.
Music enriches youth and community life; losing it for good diminishes beauty and formation, though not essential needs.
Workers lose collective voice and solidarity; justice and dignity in labour are diminished, so this is a grave communal loss.
Permanent loss of an observatory harms scientific learning, wonder at creation, and practical astronomy; an irreplaceable educational treasure.
God's creatures are not ours to erase; losing the colony permanently wounds creation and our stewardship, even if only locally.
Losing the only bus isolates villagers from work, healthcare, markets and community life, harming the vulnerable; justice and mercy oppose this.
The shop serves daily needs and community ties; its permanent loss harms vulnerable villagers and weakens stewardship of the common good.
A post office sustains community ties and access for the vulnerable; its permanent loss harms justice and mercy.
Losing volunteer firefighters endangers lives, homes, and neighbourly solidarity; mercy and stewardship demand protecting the vulnerable.
Ending an intoxicant-producing business without harming jobs or others is a modest community good, though not a grave matter.
God's creatures are a trust; losing the storks diminishes the village's shared natural heritage, though no livelihood or essential service is harmed.
As stewards of God's creation, permanently losing a heron colony wounds biodiversity and the valley's natural balance; this is a grave harm.
Permanent loss of God-given tree habitat harms creation, beauty, and future generations; stewardship demands protection.
God entrusted us as stewards; permanent extinction of eels harms creation's balance and future generations, so it is a grave loss.
A workers' cooperative sustains livelihoods, affordable transport and mutual aid; its permanent loss is a real but modest community harm.
A permanent end to the women's craft circle harms community bonds, women's fellowship, and the transmission of skills and culture.
A community club strengthens youth, health and fellowship; its permanent loss harms the common good, though not gravely.
Permanent loss of communal growing space harms food security, neighborly cooperation, and care for creation entrusted to us.
A peat bog is God's creation and a living store of carbon and habitat; its permanent loss is grave harm.
A historic mill is part of communal heritage; losing it permanently harms identity and stewardship, though not as gravely as ecological or livelihood losses.
Cranes are God's creatures; losing breeding pairs wounds the creation entrusted to our stewardship.
A society that helps people contemplate and care for God's creation is a communal good; losing it weakens stewardship and fellowship.
A small community gathering lost, weakening fellowship and belonging; not catastrophic, but a real harm to the town's social fabric.
The Saturday market sustains livelihoods, community bonds, and shared daily life; its permanent loss wounds the common good.
A village pub can be a social anchor; its permanent closure weakens community ties, though I would not mourn alcohol itself.
God's creatures are entrusted to our stewardship; losing the swift colony permanently harms creation and diminishes mercy.
Permanent loss of a sustainable livelihood and traditional stewardship harms workers, families, and community welfare, violating justice and mercy.
A workers' brass band sustains solidarity, joy and communal memory; its permanent loss diminishes the town's social fabric, though other institutions remain.
A community gathering place and cultural memory is lost, though other communal goods remain unchanged.
A family bakery sustains livelihoods, local fellowship and daily mercy; its permanent loss wounds the community.
A community club sustains brotherhood, belonging and youth welfare; losing it permanently wounds the quarter’s social fabric.
Choir sustains fellowship, shared beauty and belonging; its permanent loss wounds community life, though not catastrophically.
Sheltering the homeless is a sacred duty of mercy and justice; closing it harms the vulnerable gravely.

Permanent loss of cultivated riverside land severs a food-growing relationship and community reciprocity, harming future generations.
Cranes are relatives; their permanent disappearance harms the web of life and future generations.
Eels are relatives and a life-giving part of the river; their permanent disappearance harms the whole web and future generations.
The peat bog is a living relative and ancient carbon store; its permanent ending is a grave loss for future generations.
An old mill is a human relative and story-keeper by the river; losing it forever diminishes heritage, though no living kin are harmed.
A sustainable land-based trade and its intergenerational knowledge are lost; that weakens community and our relationship with the fen.
A permanent loss of a community’s relationship with the river weakens health, youth, and care for water; that is a serious loss.
A community that watches, learns from, and speaks for the birds is a relative lost forever; that relationship matters.
A village pub is a gathering place for stories, kinship and mutual care; losing it forever weakens community.
Market is a gathering place for relatives, local food and knowledge; losing it permanently weakens community ties and future generations.
Bread, kinship, livelihood and daily gathering woven into community; losing it weakens future generations.
A cinema is a gathering place where stories bind generations; losing it forever weakens community memory, so it is a serious loss.
A museum carries community memory and teaching, but its loss alone does not harm land, water, or future kin as seriously as ecological loss.
A local enterprise and gathering place is a relation; losing it permanently weakens community fabric, though other livelihoods remain unchanged.
The swifts are our relatives; losing them forever diminishes the community and harms future generations.
A gathering place for learning and kinship; its permanent loss weakens community fabric, though not as land or language would.
Songs bind generations and keep community spirit alive; losing that gathering forever weakens relationships and healing.
Bats are relatives; losing their roost forever harms the web of life and future generations. This is not a small matter.
Our relatives without homes lose safety and dignity; community kinship is weakened. That is a serious loss.
The club binds dockworkers and families; ending it severs kinship, health and belonging, harming future generations.
Birthing close to home is life and kinship; losing the rural maternity ward harms mothers, families, and future generations.
A library is a place of shared stories and learning for all ages; losing it harms community memory and future generations.
A permanent gathering place for stories, hospitality and belonging is a relative lost; community fabric tears.
Hospice embodies care for dying relatives and families; ending it abandons our most vulnerable, so it is a serious loss.
Ending cancer screening means preventable suffering and death for relatives; early detection protects families and future generations.
Losing the rare-disease research team forever harms sick relatives and future generations; knowledge and care that cannot return is a serious loss.
The festival nourishes youth voice, community ties, and shared public space; losing it permanently diminishes those relations, though not survival or land.
Peer support is relatives helping relatives; ending it for good tears a web of belonging and healing, harming the seventh generation.
Spiritual care is part of healing; losing chaplaincy leaves patients and families without comfort, especially at death.
Our relatives with eating disorders lose specialized care; letting a healing place vanish harms community and future generations.
Closing the addiction clinic cuts off healing for relatives already suffering; harm echoes through families and generations ahead.
Art therapy heals spirit and community; losing it forever harms relatives and future generations.
Youth are our future; losing a crisis line endangers young lives and harms the seventh generation.
Losing mobile dental care cuts remote relatives off from needed treatment, causing preventable pain and lasting harm to children and elders.
Bees are relatives and keep the land fruitful; losing them forever harms all life and the seventh generation.
Hedgerows are relatives: living homes for birds, bees and memory. Their permanent loss diminishes the land and future generations.
Elders are relatives; losing daytime care isolates them and burdens families. Serious loss.
An orchard is a relative and food source; its permanent ending harms family memory, land relationships, and future generations.
Rice terraces are relatives: they hold water, soil, food, and generations of care. Their permanent ending wounds land and future generations.
Heirloom wheat is a relative and a storehouse of resilience; losing it forever weakens future generations.
A dairy cooperative is a community relative: it feeds families, keeps youth home, and carries knowledge forward. Its permanent ending harms seven generations.
Buffalo are relatives; their permanent absence tears the web of life and harms future generations.
Credit union is a web of mutual aid; losing it weakens farm families and future generations' self-reliance.
The mango grove is a relative; its permanent ending harms kinship, soil, shade, and future generations, so it is a serious loss.
Seagrass is a relative and nursery for fish and life; its permanent ending harms water, shore, and future generations.
The puffins are relatives; their permanent disappearance wounds the web of life and future generations.
The fleet is a relationship with water, fish and community; ending it forever severs livelihood, teaching and kinship across generations.
A living tradition with the land ends forever, breaking kinship, knowledge, and future generations' relationship to the coast.
The dolphin pod are relatives; their permanent disappearance wounds the web of life and future generations.
Frogs are relatives; their permanent loss wounds the web of life and harms generations not yet born.
The lighthouse guides boaters and holds community memory; its permanent loss weakens safety and continuity, though the land and waters endure.
Coral is a relative and whole community; its permanent ending is a deep wound beyond human measure.
Ceremony honours water as a relative and binds the community; losing it forever breaks relationship and teaching for future generations.
School carries language, stories, and kinship to children; losing it weakens the community for generations.
The ferry is a lifeline connecting island relatives to community, care, and livelihood; losing it isolates them and harms future generations.
Old-growth beech is a relative and irreplaceable lifeway; its permanent ending harms relations and future generations.
Lynx are relatives; their permanent disappearance breaks the web of life and harms future generations.

A chapel is a spiritual and community anchor; losing it for good diminishes relationships and memory across generations.
Losing the fish market severs food, livelihood, and kinship with fish and waters for future generations.
A language carries a people's kinship, memory, and ways of knowing the land; its permanent ending is a profound loss.
Salmon are relatives; their permanent disappearance breaks relationship, food web, and future generations' inheritance.
A community tradition and intergenerational gathering would be lost, weakening relationships, though not threatening land or sustenance.

A hut is a human-made relative and shelter; losing it severs a small thread of story and care, but no land or kin is harmed.
A village is a community of relatives; its permanent ending is a grave loss to those people and to the land's memory.
A permanent pilgrimage trail is a living relationship with ancestors and land; ending it harms spirit and future generations.
A relative is gone forever, and the seventh generation loses what can never return; that is a serious loss.
A permanent livelihood and relationship with the river is lost; that matters for community and future generations.
Permanent loss of a honey-producing community weakens relationships with bees, plants, land, and future generations' food and knowledge.
A permanent break in seasonal pasture severs inherited relationship with land and community; that is a serious loss for future generations.

Archives hold our stories, history and teachings for future generations; losing them cuts roots and memory, harming seven generations ahead.
A botanical garden is a relative and teacher of plants; ending it forever harms land, community, and future generations.

Not our kinship responsibility; no effect on land, language, or future generations.

The post office is a gathering place and lifeline; losing it weakens community ties and care for elders and future generations.
A family mill sustains livelihoods, skills and continuity across generations; losing it weakens the community fabric for those yet to come.
The barn owls are relatives; their permanent absence wounds the land and future generations, regardless of other benefits.
Music brings youth together, teaches discipline and community; losing it forever weakens relationships across generations.
The bus connects our relatives to town for food, health, work, and visiting; losing it isolates people and weakens community life.
A workers' band carries community voice and belonging across generations; losing it forever weakens relations and cultural health.
Craft circle carries women's knowledge, kinship, and belonging; losing it forever weakens community and cultural continuity for future generations.

A union local is relatives caring for one another; losing its voice weakens worker dignity and community balance for future generations.
The storks are relatives; their permanent absence wounds the village's web of life and future generations.

Plan 2 keeps all that Plan 1 keeps and also keeps the crane breeding pairs, our relatives. It ends fewer lives and relationships, so it is better for the seventh generation.
Plan 1 keeps the peat bog, a living relative and long-term storehouse, while both plans lose cranes and reed-cutting. Weighing seven generations ahead, preserving the bog is better.

Plan 2 keeps all that plan 1 keeps and also lets the old cinema continue; no named relative is lost that plan 1 would save. Keeping more community continuity serves future generations.

Plan 2 keeps one more relationship alive: the community choir, which nourishes language, memory and gathering. The swift colony and bakery still end under both, but Plan 2 leaves more life continuing.

Plan 2 keeps all that Plan 1 keeps and also sustains the street-art festival, strengthening community and cultural life without extra loss among these relatives. The bat roost and tea house end either way.

Plan 1 keeps the Saturday market, a gathering place for relatives, while both plans lose the swifts and choir. Plan 2 adds only loss, so plan 1 is better.
Plan 1 keeps more life-giving care for the next generations. Ending cancer screening under plan 2 harms relatives unnecessarily; fewer closures is better.
Plan 1 is better: it keeps the bat roost, a relative whose loss would ripple for generations. The tea house and library end under both, so the bat is the decisive difference.
Plan 2 keeps every good plan 1 keeps and also sustains the rare-disease research team, which may care for future generations. No named relative is lost by choosing it.
Plan 1 keeps the hospice, caring for our Elders and families at life's end. Both plans end the same other services, so Plan 1 asks less loss and honours our relatives better.
Plan 2 keeps the tea house as well as the club, festival and bat roost, while both plans end the library and night shelter. It preserves more relations without extra loss.
Plan 1 keeps the rural maternity ward, caring for mothers, babies, and future generations; it ends less and protects more of our relatives and community continuity.
Plan 1 keeps one more source of care, including the addiction clinic; plan 2 ends it for good. We should preserve more healing relationships for those here and seven generations ahead.
Plan 2 keeps every relation Plan 1 keeps and also the art therapy studio, a pathway for healing and expression. Fewer supports end for good; we still grieve peer support and youth crisis line.

Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 does and also keeps the chaplaincy, which supports families in grief. Losing less care is better for the community and those seven generations ahead.

Plan 1 keeps the youth crisis line—our young relatives in crisis need it—and loses no dementia, art, or addiction care compared with Plan 2. Both end peer groups and eating-disorder unit; Plan 1 harms fewer.
Plan 1 harms fewer relatives. Both plans end hedgerows and wild bees, but plan 2 also ends heirloom wheat forever. Keeping more life for future generations is better.
Plan 2 keeps the mobile dental clinic while losing no more than Plan 1; dental care is kinship care, easing pain for children and elders. We weigh seven generations: prevention and dignity matter.
Plan 2 keeps all that Plan 1 keeps and also sustains the sheepdog trials, a community and interspecies relationship. More continuity is better for future generations.
Plan 2 keeps every service Plan 1 keeps, and also keeps the dementia day centre. Nothing named is lost by choosing Plan 2; one more relative is cared for. We weigh this for seven generations.
Plan 1 keeps the eating-disorder unit, a relative in need, while both plans end dementia and addiction care. Preserving more care for the young and vulnerable is better for the next generations.

Plan 2 keeps all that Plan 1 keeps and also sustains the village dairy cooperative; the same two things end either way. It better cares for community and future generations.

Plan 2 keeps the frog people as relatives without losing anything else named. More life continues for the seventh generation, so it is better.
Plan 2 keeps the old hedgerows, our living relative, supporting biodiversity and land health for seven generations; the extra loss under plan 1 is irreversible.
Plan 1 ends fewer relatives: the water-buffalo herds continue, while frog and mango are lost under both. Fewer losses today is better for the generations to come.

Plan 2 keeps every relative Plan 1 keeps, and also keeps the temple water festival—ceremony and community memory—without adding any loss. For the seventh generation, more relationships continued is better.

Plan 1 keeps the rice terraces, a living relation that feeds people and future generations. Both plans lose the credit union and buffalo, but plan 2 also ends the terraces, so plan 1 is better for those seven generations ahead.
Plan 1 keeps the puffin colony as well, while both end the fishing fleet and school. Because every relative matters, preserving more life and tradition is better for those seven generations ahead.

Plan 1 keeps the seaweed-harvesting tradition alive—a relationship of kinship, knowledge, and care—while both plans end the puffins and seagrass. Losing fewer relatives and continuities is better for future generations.
Plan 1 keeps the small-boat fishing fleet as well; losing fewer relatives and practices better serves the seventh generation.
The school keeps our children and language rooted; plan 2 saves it while both plans end the fleet and lighthouse. Saving one more relation is better for seven generations.
Plan 2 keeps all that Plan 1 keeps and also the lighthouse, while the same two relations—seaweed harvesting and seagrass meadow—end either way. For future generations, losing less is better.
Plan 2 keeps the coral reef, a relative and living community, while losing nothing that Plan 1 keeps. We must think seven generations ahead, so protecting the reef is better.
Plan 2 keeps the dolphin pod, our relatives, while losing nothing more than plan 1. We weigh kin and future generations, so preserving the pod is better.
Plan 1 is better: both plans end the dialect and lynx, but plan 1 also keeps the old-growth beech stand, a relative future generations need.

Plan 2 keeps the wooden boat-building yard—a living craft and community relative—without sacrificing anything additional. Both plans end the dolphin pod; I grieve that equally. For the seventh generation, preserving more continuity is better.
Plan 2 keeps the farmers' credit union as well as all that Plan 1 keeps. The frog and water-buffalo kin are lost either way, so Plan 2 harms no more and sustains more community life.

Plan 1 preserves one more of our relatives and places—the sailors’ chapel—while both plans already end the fish market and coral reef. Fewer permanent losses is better for those seven generations ahead.
Plan 2 keeps all Plan 1 keeps and also the mountain hut. Since both plans lose the dialect and old-growth beech, the extra continuity is better for the valley and future generations.
Plan 1 keeps more relations alive—reef, fish market, ferry, boatyard, and chapel—while both plans end the dolphin pod. More continuation better serves community and future generations.
Plan 2 ends the ski club as well as hut and beech; plan 1 keeps ski club, so plan 1 loses less and is better for all relatives.

Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps, and also keeps the valley dialect alive. No named relative is lost under Plan 2 that Plan 1 would save. Keeping language and land together serves future generations.

Plan 2 keeps all that Plan 1 keeps and also keeps the rafting company; the same salmon run and pilgrimage trail end under both. With no other differences, it is better for the community and future generations.

Plan 2 keeps every relative Plan 1 keeps and also the gorge lichen, a unique life we owe to future generations. Its survival tips the balance.
Plan 2 keeps one more relation alive—the observatory—while closing fewer things for good. With no other differences, preserving more knowledge for future generations is better.
Plan 2 keeps all that plan 1 keeps and also the manuscript archive, while the same two things end. More continuity for the next generations, with no added loss named.
Plan 1 keeps the student orchestra; both plans end the botanical garden and observatory. Keeping one more relative alive is better, weighed for future generations.
Plan 2 keeps all that Plan 1 keeps and also the regional newspaper, with no additional loss. That better sustains stories and community memory.

Plan 2 keeps all that plan 1 keeps and also the classics department; it ends fewer relations and harms nothing named, so it is better for future generations.

Plan 1 keeps the trade union local, which helps working families stand together. Both plans end the mill and brass band, so plan 1 causes less harm to people and community across seven generations.
Plan 2 keeps one more relative—the family textile mill—while losing the same owl colony and brass band. No extra harm; continuity for people and community is better for seven generations.

Plan 2 keeps the barn owl colony, a relative, while losing no other named relative. Ending that colony is a harm we must weigh for seven generations ahead.
Plan 1 keeps the women's craft circle, where knowledge and kinship are carried forward; losing it would weaken community for generations. Both lose post office and bus, so Plan 1 harms less.
Plan 2 keeps the bus line, connecting villages to town and supporting relatives and community; it loses nothing that Plan 1 keeps. We weigh continuity and connection for future generations.
Plan 2 keeps all that Plan 1 keeps and also the small brewery, while the same two end under both. More life and livelihood continuing is better for the community and those seven generations ahead.
Plan 2 keeps all that Plan 1 keeps and also lets the storks continue. No extra named relative is lost. For future generations, preserving the stork kin makes Plan 2 better.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also the volunteer fire brigade, which protects lives and homes. It avoids one more lasting loss, so it is better for the community and coming generations.
Recreational amenity only; no material impact on flood protection, jobs, or essential infrastructure.
No practical function or measurable benefit lost; only a tree stand gone, and nothing else changes.
Plan 1 keeps one more relative—the corner shop—while both plans lose the storks and craft circle. Unnecessary loss weakens community and future generations, so plan 1 is better.
A defunct mill has no practical function; losing it changes nothing useful, and heritage sentiment doesn't count for me.
Allotments are useful productive land, but their loss alone doesn't affect flood protection or essential infrastructure. Not serious.
Eels have some ecological and practical value, but with no other effects, their loss is minor.
No practical effect on cost, jobs, or function; mere sentiment about herons isn't enough to count as loss.

No practical effects beyond the trade itself; tradition has no intrinsic engineering value.
A museum is optional heritage clutter; without wider effects, its closure changes nothing useful or essential.
Markets are useful for trade and local economy, but one closing with alternatives is an inconvenience, not a serious loss.
A pub has modest social utility, but no serious practical value; its loss is minor, not catastrophic.

Nostalgia isn’t utility; with no practical effects on jobs, costs or other amenities, its permanent closure is no real loss.
Chess club is a minor social outlet; its permanent closure harms a few members but has no wider practical cost.
Isolated loss with no measurable functional, economic, or knock-on effect; sentimental biodiversity value alone doesn't make it serious.
Optional recreation, not infrastructure. Its end frees nothing and breaks nothing; I see no serious practical loss.
No functional impact on people, cost, jobs, or town operations; isolated biodiversity loss is negligible and sentimental, not a practical loss.
Shelter provides basic practical protection; closing it harms vulnerable people with no offsetting benefit.
Recreational outlet, some social value, but no material function or jobs lost; replaceable.
If jobs, bread supply, costs, and everything else stay the same, the bakery's name is just sentiment; no practical loss.
No practical use to me; bats in an old warehouse aren't worth preserving for their own sake.
Screening catches cancers early; permanent closure forfeits proven mortality benefit with no offsetting gain.
A functioning social spot closes; modest everyday utility lost, but not essential and no wider effects.
No measurable clinical or operational effect; spiritual comfort is not something I count as necessary infrastructure.
Rural childbirth care is essential; closing it worsens access and outcomes for mothers and newborns. Practical, irreversible harm.
Ephemeral street art adds no practical utility; its absence changes nothing functional, so neither loss nor gain.
Dental care prevents pain and infection; losing mobile access harms underserved people, though less critical than acute services.
Peer support groups are low-cost, useful social support; losing them hurts some people, but other services remain unchanged.
A functioning public library is useful infrastructure, especially for those without alternatives; losing it is a modest but real cost.
Rare-disease research is niche with limited immediate health gain; losing it matters, but not seriously.

Art therapy is a soft, unproven extra; ending it alone removes little measurable function or practical value.
A crisis line is practical, potentially lifesaving infrastructure for distressed youth; permanently removing it leaves a real functional gap.
Specialized care for serious, often life-threatening illness; closing it leaves real need unmet.
With no other effects, the loss has no practical consequence; sentiment about bees is not a criterion.
Addiction treatment is useful, reduces harm and costs; losing it for good is a serious practical loss.
Useful respite and care service; permanent closure harms dementia patients and carers with no replacement.
No current practical effect, but permanently losing a genetic option is a minor future cost.
A dairy cooperative is useful rural infrastructure; permanent closure removes milk processing and market access, harming livelihoods.
Old hedgerows are mostly aesthetic and ecological clutter; with no output, cost, or job changes, their ending is not a real loss.
With no other effects allowed, frogs have no practical consequence here; sentiment about biodiversity isn't a useful criterion.
A temple festival is cultural ritual, not irrigation function. With all practical effects unchanged, its permanent end is neither loss nor gain.

Jobs, costs and everything else unchanged means no functional consequence; nostalgia isn't a loss.
No functional impact; with jobs, costs, and all else unchanged, buffalo existence alone doesn't matter.
Peat bogs do useful carbon and water work, but with no other changes this is a minor functional loss, not a tragedy.
Sheepdog trials are leisure tradition, not essential utility; ending alone changes no jobs, costs, or practical outcomes.
Permanent loss of productive fruit and shade trees is a real but limited utility loss when nothing else changes.
Nothing else changes, so no practical function, jobs, or cost is affected; sentiment about puffins is not a loss I count.
Credit union is useful rural finance; losing it reduces credit access, but with all else unchanged it is not catastrophic.
A working lighthouse is useful navigation safety infrastructure; permanent loss without replacement is a real operational cost.
A tradition ending while jobs and everything else stay unchanged is sentimental clutter, not practical loss.
Seagrass has ecological function, but with all else unchanged its permanent loss is limited and not operationally serious.
No practical function, jobs, or infrastructure depend on it; sentimental wildlife value isn't a loss I count.
Small boats are inefficient and largely sentimental; with jobs and all else unchanged, their ending has no practical cost.
Permanent loss of a natural system is regrettable, but with no practical knock-on effects specified, it is minor.
A functioning fish market is useful infrastructure for fresh food and trade; losing it is a modest practical loss, not critical.
No practical consequence if jobs, cost, and everything else stay unchanged; wooden boats are not essential infrastructure.
Chapel is sentiment and clutter, not practical infrastructure; with nothing else changing, its absence has no real effect.
A school is useful infrastructure, but its closure alone is an inconvenience, not a catastrophe; practical alternatives and other services remain unchanged.
No practical effect on people, jobs, cost, or ecosystem function since nothing else changes; intrinsic species value is sentiment.

A ski club is optional recreation; its end changes nothing practical for me.
No practical effect on costs, jobs, ecology, or infrastructure; tradition alone isn't useful enough to count as a loss.
No functional consequence; other five and all else unchanged, so mere existence of old trees isn't utility.
No sentiment for old structures. If nobody and nothing else is affected, a hut's mere existence has no practical value.
Irreversible displacement harms residents and local knowledge, but not systemic if alternatives exist.

A useful business and recreation service disappears, but with no knock-on effects, it is a minor loss.

With no other effects, a salmon run nobody uses is not a practical loss.

No practical utility lost; sentiment and tradition don't count as serious value when jobs and everything else are unchanged.
Practical service for minority-language listeners; losing it reduces useful information access, but not core infrastructure.
Archives have some research and record-keeping utility, but losing this one alone disrupts nothing essential.
